The new house is established; the picture of Saint Anne is needed, and Vincenza should send it quickly. She is to welcome the two postulants, both good, and have them prepared; one can help the girls of the Poss factory in their spiritual formation and in running the Congregation of the Children of Mary established there. She is to record the postulants' accounts exactly and keep everything in order, because she must go and visit the house at Foligno.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I received your long letter through Sr. A. Paola. As for what you tell me about the postulant, do write that they should come and fetch her; you have done well in everything else too, [I am] very pleased.1

2. So, there is a house of the Daughters of Saint Anne here and the Chapel must soon be set up, and you will send me the picture of Saint Anne; have a small frame put on it, then put it in the crate and send it to the address of the Parish Priest [of] Vespolate that I sent you,2 as I have already given you; put inside the flower paper that Paola had left over, so that some flowers can be made here for this poor oratory, which has still to be set up.

3. Listen, you will receive this letter of mine from the hands of a 4th-grade certified teacher, a very dear person; I commend her warmly to you; give her a bed with a good mattress and curtains; she wishes to revise her studies a little. Let Sr. Anna Eletta take her on, have her revise them and give her good teaching; then we shall clothe her

soon; being with you she will learn and become a good religious; we may also be able to use her as a Superior.3

4. I hear about that person; he does well to enjoy himself.4 My dear Vincenza, there is as much work as one could want.

5. You are right that Providence does not seem to want to come to us through postulants. Listen, do write to the one from S. Arcangelo to bring the 1,000 F. in cash; explain yourself clearly, because, you know, sometimes these creatures bring in rags in place of money; not that; otherwise, let her come at once with 1,000 F. in cash and her outfit, cloth and linen, whatever she has.5

6. Be careful to note down well those postulants who still owe; have proper receipts made out on stamped paper with the date for this payment clearly fixed; do not forget, because unfortunately some of these hundred F. have gone astray.6 If a little store could be laid in for the winter, especially of grain and maize, enough. Let us pray, for the Lord will give us what we need.

7. So the Clothing can be performed by Father Mancini; and the one who comes with the teacher you will likewise put in a curtained bed, and she too will be clothed, for she will serve for Poss, for the girls' school, for spiritual matters, and likewise for the Children of Mary: she will encourage them, gather them, and you will see that the Congregation will be firmly founded; this pleases Mary and Saint Anne. You will clothe her and then put her to work; she will draw them.7

8. You must write to Soresina to send you girls, but let them see to it that they have a doctor's certificate that they are healthy and grown up; that is what you must look for; otherwise accept them; I shall try to do the same, and Poss may rest easy.8

9. See whether you could get that poor girl who came, from Piacenza, and whether she could be accepted; now she keeps coming to my mind; I am very sorry I sent her away. Have Mancini's girls not arrived yet?9

10. Address your letters to Ovada, but mind, I shall stay there only three days, so plan accordingly; you can send the exercise books and all the books so that she can study; but it is enough to send the picture with the flower things inside; that is enough; the rest will be brought by those who are to come later.10

11. My dear daughter, for charity's sake, try to get everything ready and in order, for as soon as Mancini comes, whom you will put in the Father's room, you will have to go to Foligno and also to S. Martinello, for things there are boiling over like a cauldron.11 First it would be neces-

sary for me to speak to you. Oh, how it pains me that you are tied down by the Holy Retreat, you cannot believe it! I am truly on thorns about Foligno, because it would be very good for you to leave at once, for no good would come of that Sup. knowing;12 enough, in person; it means you can come over here for a moment. Goodbye, your affectionate

M. R.

1 This letter has not been preserved. There is, however, the one of 18.9, in reply

to the present one.

2 Cf. L 320,3.

3 From the hands of a certified teacher. It cannot be determined precisely

from the Postulants' Register who she is.

4 Sr. A. Vincenza had informed her (on 11.9.74): “Fr Tornatore is going to the coun-

try today and will not be back until next Saturday”.

5 The one from S. Arcangelo: Margherita Casalini. When presenting her they said they

would pay F. 3,000, but then they had reduced the figure. They bring in

rags: they bring clothing of little value (rags) instead of money.

6 Sr. A. Vincenza gives her an account of the fees brought by the individual pos-

tulants (two of hers and seven of Fr Mancini's) and of how much they undertake to pay in later

instalments.

7 The clothing may be presided over by Fr Giovanni Mancini. (Cf. L 315,

n. 9). Likewise the young woman coming from Invorio with the teacher, mentioned above

in para. 3. She will be a good formator of the girls who work in the

Poss factory; she will draw them, guide them and encourage them in goodness.

8 you must write to the parish priest of Soresina, Fr Luigi Malfina, to send

girls for the Poss works, provided they have the requirements for

being taken on.

9 Mancini's girls arrived on 18 September.

10 To Invorio you can send, etc.; but it is enough: as for the other things, send

only the picture of Saint Anne and the paper for making flowers for the chapel.

11 Prepare in good time the welcome for Fr Mancini and everything else, because then

she will have to go to Foligno, where things are boiling like a cauldron under pressure, and

to S. Martinello.

12 She leaves the sentence unfinished. The explanation of the unpleasant situation

would be too long. She will speak to her about it.

She is at Ovada, where she will stay three days; she again commends the two postulants to her.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Here we are, arrived at Ovada, and on Monday morning [in Genoa] I hope to find letters from you there. I am still on my feet; please let that Person know that if he wants to write to me he should address the letters to Genoa, for I am sure he will write; I am not writing to him because I am tired of writing.1

2. Greet Carlotta for me; have the postulants reached you? I commend them both to you; I would like them to be happy, and the lame one to be able to write to the Bishop that she is happy; let her write wherever she likes. I hope she will write that she is happy; if that person comes, let him speak a little to both of them, especially to one.3 That is enough for now; I shall write to you at Genoa, where I hope to find letters from you. I am in a hurry, your

affectionate M.

1 Here we are: on the 18th they arrived at Ovada (Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega is with her);

on the 21st they will be in Genoa... let... know: the message is for Fr Tornatore.

2 the postulants from Invorio; to the Bishop of Novara, Mgr Giacomo Gentile.

3 Let Fr Tornatore speak to them a little and form them for religious life.

In two days she will be at Sampierdarena; she cannot tell her the exact time.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. God willing, on Monday I shall be in your arms; I shall get off at S. P. d'Arena on purpose;1 I cannot tell you the time because I want to go by way of Voltri, but I shall come to the Hospital as soon as I get off. I have received the newspaper; everything in person;2 I must go, for the carriage is here to take me to the Bishop at Strevi.3 I have been travelling since Monday; I am all of a heap.4

Goodbye; greet everyone for me, and believe me yours

Affectionately, M. R.

1 Monday, 21 September; I want to go by way of Voltri (near Genoa).

2 The newspaper: cf. L 316, n. 2.

3 I am going to the Bishop at Strevi (Alessandria).

4 all a heap of aches from great fatigue.

She instructs her to send two Sisters to Piacenza.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. God willing, on Monday I shall be at S. P. d'Arena and then Genoa.1 I am writing in haste: send Sr. A. Palmira and Sr. A. Virginia to Piacenza at once. I hope you will certainly send them on Monday, as this letter will reach you tomorrow.2

Greet everyone; I am

your affectionate M. R.

1 Cf. L 323,1.

2 She has Sr. A. Palmira Grillotti and Sr. A. Virginia

Gaggi leave for Piacenza at once.

She accepts his proposal to take on the schools and sets out certain indispensable conditions for acceptance.

Reverend Parish Priest,

1. Forgive me for not answering your most esteemed letter by return of post; the reason was my absence. I very willingly accept the direction of the schools that Your Very Reverend Lordship proposes to me.2

2. I need only let you know that we cannot go fewer than four, or three at the very least, and also that the stipend you propose is too little; it should be at least 1,200 f. If Your Reverence agrees to this, write to me the day on which I am to send them and I will send them to you at once.3

In the hope of a letter from you, whether confirming or declining, believe me, with all esteem and reverence,

Your most humble Servant, Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 The Mother was at Ovada, but was to go to Genoa on 21 September;

so she dated the letter from Genoa.

2 The direction of the Schools at Montefiorino (Modena).

3 write to me: she lets him understand that her answer is positive.

She encloses a letter for the Father, answers some of her questions and asks for prayers, from the community as well, for the conversion of a Priest who is in the Sampierdarena Hospital with a serious illness.

A.M.F. Dear daughter,

1. A line in haste; tomorrow I leave for Genoa, where I shall be at 12/13 in the afternoon. Write to me at the Genoa house. Today, as I write, you will have that Person there; give him this.2

2. You ask me about the postulant's brother, the Priest: yes, let him come and attend the ceremony.3

3. You tell me about the accounts. My God! Enough, I am at peace, everything will come to you.4

4. Has Carlotta gone to Genoa?5 Goodbye.

5. Greet everyone for me and have prayers said for the journey, and also a novena for the conversion of a Priest who is in the hospital at S. P. d'Arena, who became a Protestant and now has cancer of the tongue and will hear of nothing. I commend him to you earnestly; tell the postulants, the religious, that person; meanwhile, a novena.

6. This too, in silence, you will tell the person, about Foligno.6 Alas, dear Vincenza, what troubles there are! Enough, [I entrust myself] to our little mother of the Sacred Heart of Jesus; She will set everything right for me; and pray. Goodbye.

7. For charity's sake, let Carlotta not leave Onorata's side, and I would not like her to go to the Countess's alone.7

[Your affectionate MOTHER ROSA]

The date is deduced from the context.

On the 21st, Monday. Give the enclosed letter to Fr Tornatore. The brother of the Postulant Elena Merli, from Cortemaggiore. The clothing took place on 29 September.

4 the accounts. Vincenza had written to her on the 18th: “I gave the mason F. 200, but

how much there still is! The carpenter also gave me his account and it comes to F. 600”. The

Mother learns this with pain: my God! But she adds confidently: everything will

come to you, providence will come to pay it all.

5 She does not yet know anything definite about the departure. On 11 September Sr. A. Vin-

cenza had told her that they (Carlotta and Onorata Colli) would leave for

Genoa on 15 or 16 September.

6 You will tell Fr Tornatore, in secret, about the unpleasant situation at Foligno.

(Cf. L 321,11).

7 Carlotta was warmly received by Countess Edvige Marazzani and gladly

went to her palazzo.

She speaks of two girls to be sent to Genoa. At Cortemaggiore difficulties have arisen between the Hospital Administration and the two Communities. She asks her forgiveness for not having shown her all the attention she deserved, encourages her and invites her to join her in Genoa after pressing for the examinations to be held.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Here we are at S. P. d'Arena; I am writing to you in my own hand so that you may be convinced that I am well and have had [a good journey]; it is very late and I am writing to you on my knees.

2. Listen: 1st, tell that person that I received his letter at Ovada; 2nd, see whether that girl from Genoa who was ill in the hospital, the one who was so naughty, if by ill luck she has come out and is not behaving, you could send her, and also that other one who is always poorly, send her away too, as she [is] from Genoa; you could send them to Sr. A. Elvira, for they need them here.2

3. Patience, I made a mistake; what can I say? my dear, I am a dolt. The father of the postulant you wrote to brought us F. 40, which I am keeping.3

4. Give this letter from Insani to that Person, but tell him it is not true that Sr. A. Tina wants money and said he should have it asked of me.4 Enough; do you know what has happened meanwhile? They made it known that the Superior of the hospital helps the other, and so

the Administration raised an uproar without equal and the village is saying all sorts of things,5 and in the hospital they now want only 4 Sisters, and moreover the hospital Sisters are no longer to go to those at the Maddalena, and those cannot go to the hospital any more, and a fine mess has been made of it. My God!6

5. Dear Vincenza, you know, I have a scruple at having always been so disobliging to you; you showed me a thousand attentions and I always mortified you. How I suffer for this courtesy of mine, God alone sees; meanwhile I ask your forgiveness and hope with God's help never to do such things again.7

6. Yes, clothe all those you think fit, for I shall always approve everything.8 Do everything with courage and do not fret. When you have held the clothing, come to Genoa; I shall write to tell you whom to bring me.

7. Listen, see about pressing for the examinations, because I would need to send them by the middle of October. Ask the Inspector, and the Priest too, to whom I hope you will have sent the present.9

8. I would like you to give French lessons to Sr. A. Eletta, because I must send her as teacher to Invorio; but silence, for charity's sake, let no one know; I hope a few lessons will be enough for her. The Superior Sr. Filomena will come to you and you will put her at the Morte,10 so that Sr. A. Eufemia will be free, for she will have to leave as soon as she has taken her examinations.11

Goodbye, yours in haste, affectionately for ever,

MOTHER ROSA. Address your letters to Genoa.

1 The date is incomplete, but the month and year are easily identified from the

content.

2 Sr. A. Vincenza replies (on 23.9) that she will send them both to

Genoa, accompanied by Sr. A. Elvira Persiani.

3 I made a mistake... Reading these expressions and the others in para. 5, her daughter

is astonished: “My Mother, whatever is this! you were not yourself when you wrote such things. My

God, I who caused you so much grief, ah, if you could feel the pain it gives me!”.

4 you will give Canon Stefano Insani's letter to Fr Tornatore.

5 Cf. L 328, n. 3 and 4.

6 those at the Maddalena: the Sisters of the other community, devoted to nursing

the sick at home, who are guests of Signora Maddalena Parmigiani. Cf.

L 328.

7 always disobliging: I did not know how to repay you, I was ungrateful;

how I suffer for this discourteous way of behaving.

8 The clothing took place at the end of the Spiritual Exercises preached by

Fr Mancini (L Sr. A. Vincenza to M. Rosa, 23.9.74), on 29 September.

9 The examinations were held on 20 October (cf. L Rapallino to M. Rosa, 1.10.74).

And the Priest: presumably a member of the Board.

10 Sup. Filomena Pugnaloni is assigned to the house in Via della Morte.

11 Sr. A. Eufemia Camporesi was to complete her studies in preparation

for the teaching certificate examinations.

She has been informed of their displeasure at the two supernumerary Sisters in the Hospital. She explains her reasons and assures them she has withdrawn them.

[Mr President]2

1. I have received letters from the Superior informing me that Your Most Illustrious Lordships are displeased at having more Sisters in your Hospital (than) the agreed number.3 I did this so that the patients might be better cared for and the Sisters more relieved of fatigue; it was, moreover, a gift that the Daughters of Saint Anne were making to this Hospital entirely at their own expense.

2. Since Your Most Illustrious Lordships do not welcome this – whereas all the other Hospitals would ask nothing better than that we increase the Sisters at our expense – I have already ordered the said Superior to send the two extra Sisters to Piacenza, and likewise to cut off communication between Signora Maddalena's house and the Hospital.4

3. I would ask the Administration kindly to send me a line for my guidance. Please accept the sentiments of deep esteem and respect of one who is honoured to call herself Your Most Illustrious Lordships'

most humble Servant, Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 The date is deduced from the context.

2 President of the hospital, Signor Luigi Parmigiani.

3 The Superior Tommasina Viterbo had informed her on 15 Septem-

ber of the complaint made to her about the excess number of Sisters: six instead of the four

required by the contract.

4 cut off communication: the said Superior also told her of

another cause of discontent: “in the village they say that the Sisters (of the other commu-

nity) come and eat the hospital's food, and if I sometimes send them some-

thing they say I keep them on the hospital's goods”.

3-

O

Cortemaggiore – Hospital: a ward.

From her letter she hears how providence is helping her. She is pleased with the good news about Fr Mancini; tell him to call the Daughters of Saint Anne to Paris. Two chasubles must be sent to Invorio. She has much work, but plans to go to Piacenza at the end of the month for just two days. She needs to speak to her before sending her to Terricciola and S. Martinello.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received your letter and hear how providence is helping you; I hope you will pay the accounts; by now you will have received my second letter, in which I sent you Insani's, and you will have heard how the muddle happened; enough. God, I hope, will put it right.1

2. I am very glad of the good news you give me of Father Mancini; tell him to call us to Paris; I approve all you have done, you do everything well; courage, and do not go about things fearfully.2

3. I have not even time to breathe, so weighed down am I with work; do not think I do this for any other reason, because if you saw me you would certainly be dumbfounded. Perhaps on Monday you can manage it: send the old red chasuble, the one I had repaired, which is spare, and also the old white one, which is spare, to Invorio Inferiore, to the Superior; I am sending the rest from here.3

4. Goodbye, I have too much work. “My God, give me a hundred arms, that I may wear them all out for you”.4

5. Probably at the end of October I shall slip away to

Piacenza for 48 hours, without saying anything. There are too many things I must tell you, and you must go to Terricciola and S. Martinello.5

Your affectionate M. R. Many greetings to all. Goodbye, my dear.

1 your letter: it is dated 23.9.74; providence is helping you. There had been an in-

come of 800 F. My second: L 327.

2 “Fr Mancini is ever more enthusiastic about the Daughters of Saint Anne and is so

happy here... he says he feels he is in Paradise... he says he could listen to us

praying for ever.” He – writes Vincenza – was about to go to Paris.

3 Perhaps on Monday you can manage it: send to the Superior Paola Buc-

ciotti at Invorio the red and the white chasubles that are spare, which we do not

need.

4 My God... for you: a concise and telling expression.

5 To Terricciola (Pisa) and S. Martinello – Perugia, two communities that were

to be opened.

She instructs her to send two nurses to Rome and also to send an alb to Invorio, where the Bishop wants the clothing of the six postulants to take place. She has an eye infection and finds it hard to write.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Today, a minute's time after writing eight letters, so that I can no1 longer even feel my stomach. I still need to write to you to tell you many things. Listen, for charity's sake, send two nurses to Rome quickly: Sr. A. Geltrude – if she is better – and Sr. A. Cunegonda. If Geltrude is not well, then replace her with another from Cortemaggiore, but not from Maddalena's house,2 rather from the hospital, and a good one. Signora Elisa will go too.

2. You would need to send, do send an alb to Invorio; the rest, corporals, amices, etc., I am sending from here.3

3. Listen, you would need to send her the form for the clothing, because the Bishop wishes to clothe those six at Invorio, where they are now; then they will send them straight back to Piacenza and you will send them others. I shall let you know beforehand.4

4. I would like to write to that person, but my God! I do not know where my head is. I am going to Mamma, for they are saying Mass for the first time, and then I must be at the meeting about S. P. d'Arena.6

5. My eyes are very bad; this is the 12th letter I have written this morning alone; what is happening to me I do not know; they

hurt and give off a great deal of matter. I hope I shall soon be better. Goodbye. Greet everyone for me and believe me, in haste, your affectionate

M. R.

1 nemo: not even.

2 Sr. A. Geltrude Gottelli and Sr. A. Cunegonda Conti. Maddalena's house:

cf. L 327, n. 6.

3 Cf. L 329,3.

4 The Bishop, Mgr Giacomo Gentile. (Cf. L 322, n. 2).

5 for they are saying Mass for the first time in the house chapel.

6 at Sampierdarena she was to attend a meeting with the hospital

administrators.

Worried about her illness, she asks for news of her health and urges her to take care of herself. Vincenza has paid the debts, which pleases her. Prudence in speaking of the house's finances. She tells her the price of flour in Genoa, for her guidance.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I hear from your letter that you have had convulsions; however did it happen? What was the cause? Ah, for pity's sake, write and tell me whether the air there is making you suffer.

2. I am glad to hear that you have paid all the accounts; for charity's sake, try to eat, and drink a little wine.

3. You did well to answer that person so, and if she comes again to ask you such questions, tell her: “Madam, rest assured that I have already paid them all, and so I no longer need to talk about it”. For pity's sake, be careful, because it is a very serious matter.1

4. As for the wine, I am glad the Countess provides it for you, because it is an expense not known about.2 Flour is now very cheap;3 here the finest flour costs only F. 38 a sack, which is a quintal; this for your guidance. For charity's sake, take care of yourself, I urge you.

Goodbye; you will soon have the teacher, and I am your

affectionate M. R.

1 Signora Teresina Zagotti had asked her for “the amount of the debt, tel-

ling me that the Countess wanted to know it” – so the Superior – and she, remembering

the Mother's warning, told her nothing (cf. L 319,4).

2 an expense not known about: it is not clear what she means; perhaps not fore-

seeable.

3 Flour is cheap.

Mgr Negrotto was unfavourably impressed by the Poss factory; he may be told that everyone is enthusiastic, that many girls are on the list to start work and that much good is done there. She asks whether he has been able to cash the vouchers of two postulants. She hopes also to receive news of the Marchioness Anguissola, who is visiting Rome.

A.M.F.

My Father Agostino,

1. A minute's time, in haste, I devote entirely to you, for it seems a century since I had letters from you, and since I wrote to you. I do not know how the Poss factory made such an impression [on] Mgr N.;2 well, you can tell him that, on the contrary, everyone is very enthusiastic, and I do not know which of the first applicants to accept, and many are waiting for a place. Good is being done; it happened that the factory was empty, so it made no impression;3 enough, let us leave everything in God's hands; let Him see to what He wants in His Work.

2. Tell me whether you have been able to check the vouchers of those two; I would like to hear that they have been cashed; then you could hand them over to Sr. A. Domenica.4

3. I hope soon to receive letters from you bringing good news. I gather that you will now be tireless on behalf of the Marchioness Anguissola; who knows how many dinners you will already have enjoyed; the Archpriest will keep you good company, and the Pope will have received her with pleasure, and Mgr N. Enough, write and tell me everything, for I am anxious for news.5

Receive a sackful of greetings from all, and in particular from one who calls herself Yours for ever,

Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 The date is deduced from Fr Agostino's reply, which acknowledges receipt

on 29 September.

2 Mgr Augusto Negrotto, after visiting the houses of Genoa and Sampier-

darena, went to Piacenza and there visited the two houses and the Poss factory. But here

he was not favourably impressed (cf. L Rapallino to M. Rosa, 28.9.1874).

3 I do not know which of the first to accept: there are so many applications from

girls that she does not know whom to prefer.

4 The vouchers: of Sr. A. Elvira Persiani and Sr. A. Filomena Pugnaloni, two

Sisters from Rome; the Superior Domenica Marchesini.

5 The Marchioness Fanny Anguissola had gone to Rome with the Archpriest of

Cortemaggiore, Fr Domenico Costa. Mgr N.: Negrotto.

She has had no letters for days and fears for Vincenza's health. The two little girls and Sr. A. Filomena will have arrived. She reminds her to send Sr. A. Paola the Rules for the Confessor. Her eyes are still very bad and she has a great deal of work.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. For three days I have [received] no letters from you; I want to hope that it is as I think, that you are very busy; meanwhile the fear that it is your health will not leave me; enough.1

2. Today you will have received the two little girls, very good and hard-working, small but sturdy, and also Sr. A. Filomena, who will afterwards serve for the house of the Morte.2

3. You forgot to send Sr. A. Paola the Rules for the Confessor. See whether you are still in time; it would be good to put them in the crate with the chasubles. For charity's sake, let them not go astray.3

4. Have you sent the two nurses to Rome? Has that person come back from the country?4

5. My dear Vincenza, how much work! I do not know where I am; besides, my eyes are still very bad: all the wicked thoughts coming out through the eyelids. I write, but I assure you that in the evening it feels as if there were lots of pins in them.5 I must finish, because I am going to S. P. d'Arena, but I shall be back this evening. Goodbye. Greet everyone for me and believe me your

affectionate MOTHER 609

1 Sr. A. Vincenza had been very busy with the clothing of the postulants

(cf. L 327, n. 8).

2 Sr. A. Filomena Pugnaloni: she went as Superior to the house in Via della

Morte (cf. L 327, n. 10).

3 to Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti, the Superior of the newly opened house at Invorio

Inferiore (cf. L 320,1-3; 329,3).

4 Cf. L 330,1. That person: Fr Tornatore.

5 the wicked thoughts coming out through the eyelids: a jovial way of making light

of that ailment, which was no small matter; cf. L 330,5.

Worried about her health, she advises her to call the doctor, not to worry about debts and to ask her for whatever she needs. She need not trouble herself about the Countess: she is given a present only for Saint Anne's day. In any case, the Mother will let her know if anything needs doing.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Yesterday I received a letter from you in which you tell me you are still poorly. How it grieves me! You certainly cannot believe it, and besides, the convulsion you had keeps me in constant anxiety.2 Have you called the doctor? Listen, for pity's sake, do not go distressing yourself over the debts, because if you have no [money] I will send you some.3

2. Write and tell me, and I will send you at once whatever you need, but for pity's sake do not be upset. Write to me at once how you are; and as for Sr. A. Luigia, I shall soon remove her from you; say nothing; then you will put Sr. A. Costantina in her place and you will see she does well. All this when I send you the teachers.4

3. Do not worry about the Countess, because it was never the custom to send her anything, only on Saint Anne's day, because it is her name day. At Christmas only a letter and nothing else, do you understand? So rest easy, for if there were anything to be done I would tell you.

4. Be careful to go and pay a visit to His Eminence before he goes to Rome.5 Goodbye, in haste,

your affectionate M.

1 this must be a slip: September has 30 days.

2 Cf. L 331,1.

3 do not go distressing yourself. Sr. A. Carlotta had set herself “with great determination

and even at the cost of her life to set everything right, and perhaps this has affected her

health” – these are the exact words written to the Mother – on 28 September.

4 She has thought of removing a Sister who causes her trouble in the community.

She thanks him for the forms he sent. Her indulgenced Crucifix has been stolen, and she asks him to obtain another. She will soon send the two Sisters. She regrets the obstacles placed in the way of the service of charity. It is a time for work, but she, alas, can do very little, in such poor health as she is.

A.M.F.

My Father,

1. I have received yours with the forms inside, for collecting those small dowries. The Lord bless you for working for the Daughters of Saint Anne.1 On Saturday I go to Piacenza and shall at once have my signature authenticated by the Curia, because you know that here it is not within our reach. My Father, on every side there are sorrows and troubles; if God so wills, may he be blessed for ever.

2. Listen, while travelling, I do not know how, some zealous creatures stole my Crucifix, and I am sorry, because it had the indulgences of the Way of the Cross, so I can no longer make it; being lame, I cannot go round. My Father Agostino, buy me another and have these words written on the cross: Way of the Cross: privileged blessing in articulo mortis – so that perhaps they will be moved and not steal it. I had all the Religious questioned, and it was not they.2

3. I shall soon send the teacher for the Fornaci and the Superior for the Parrocchietta. I hope they will do good; otherwise those poor girls could fall into the hands of lay teachers and turn from dear Children of Mary into devils.

4. How it grieves me always to hear that comforts are needed in order to do a little good!3

5. “My Saviour! You who preached in the open air, you without house or roof, had nothing but the glorification of your Father; and we?”.4

6. Poor me, a real little dolt, I have never known how to do anything for this dear Redeemer; it is time to toil! I am sorry that I can do nothing myself, being always unwell, and indeed, from getting caught in the rain, I have a considerable cough.5

7. Could it be the signal for retreat? Enough, let God do as He will; all that He does is always for our good.6 Pray for me, as I do for you.

Your humble Servant, Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 the forms for collecting the small dowries of two Sisters, which he had

taken an interest in. (Cf. L 332, n. 4).

2 I had the religious questioned one by one; none of them took it.

3 how it grieves me to hear of the obstacles raised and the comforts

4 Jesus teaches us otherwise. She turns to Him, poor and itinerant, moved

solely by the glorification of the Father (Lk 9:57-58). And we? The contrast is

stark.

5 Poor me. She feels she has pointed out others' shortcomings and looks at her-

self: I can do nothing... just from being caught in the rain she has a

considerable cough.

6 for retreat? ...good. Filial abandonment to God the Father, lived in the sad

After setting out the aims and running of her charitable work, which is strictly private in character, she disputes the attempt to treat the Sampierdarena house as a Pious Work, subject to the regulations governing such Works. She therefore asks for a declaration on the nature of this Home for poor girls, so that she can take the appropriate decisions.

[Most Illustrious Prefect],

1. The undersigned, moved by the desire to be of some help to suffering humanity, gathered around her a number of women able to assist her in her aims with their means, their intelligence and their good will.

2. The Work, begun some years ago, is making progress with the approval of a great many families, for the aim of the petitioner and her companions is: 1st, to give their care to the sick in those families where it is requested; 2nd, to take in poor girls who are orphaned or abandoned, in order to give them a moral education and teach them women's work, for a small fee or free of charge.

3. The petitioner provides from her own means for all expenses and needs, without recourse either to public charity or to any of the other means on which Pious Institutes depend, whether founded through the virtue and generosity of a Pious founder or on the initiative of benevolent citizens.

4. The petitioner does not intend to give her charitable works a public character; she lives privately with her companions, and each provides from her own funds for her own par-

ticular needs or those shared with the others. She asks nothing of the Government except the personal protection to which she is entitled as a citizen and taxpayer of the State, whose laws she respects.

5. In this social condition of hers, which is contrary to no law, she cannot understand why the provisions of the law on Pious Works should be applied to the gathering of girls whom she maintains with her own money and the help of her friends, in premises she owns at Sampierdarena.

6. She believes she is not obliged to give account of her actions so long as they are not contrary to the principles of public morality and the laws of the State. Should the Government wish to compel her to submit to state supervision, she would be obliged, in order to preserve her freedom, to abandon to poverty and the dangers of corruption so many poor girls whom the undersigned has hitherto maintained and protected with her own means.

7. The petitioner therefore begs Your Excellency to declare definitively whether or not the Home for girls at Sampierdarena under the title – Daughters of Saint Anne – is a Pious Institute subject to the law on Pious Works, so that the petitioner may decide whether or not to continue the work undertaken.

The Petitioner, ROSA GATTORNO

She replies at once to her letter to reassure her. She reminds her of her promise never to go out alone and to take part in community prayer. Without prayer, work is imperfect. If Francesca loves her, as she has so often shown by deeds, she must confirm it by giving proof of a great love for God.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Today I received your letter and am writing at once to reassure you; I am a little better; the cough that still torments me will, let us hope, stop.1 My dear Francesca, remember the promise you made me never to go out alone, and also to watch over the Sisters so that they never go out alone.2

2. You promised me you would pray and be present at the Community's prayers. Yes, my dear, prayers are the adornment of our actions; what will he do if we offer our God imperfect work? He will surely set it aside and not even look at it; but if it is adorned and embellished by prayer, then it will indeed attract his gaze, and he will take delight in us.3

3. Ah, beatitude without equal, that we should be God's delight! Ah, my daughter, what joy; nothing on this earth resembles it.4

4. You have told me so many times, and shown me by deeds, your love for me, for which I am exceedingly grateful; but how happy I would be if you confirmed it by giving me proof that you love God greatly and feel a great love for Him; I assure you

that this joy would bring great relief to my burdens.5

5. Come, then, come with me to Calvary for love of our Crucified One, to be for Him alone and with Him on the Cross!6

Greet the Sisters for me, the two dentists7 and Sr. A. Elisabetta; and receive every good wish from one who calls herself your

affectionate M. R.

2 It was a prescription of the Rule not to go out alone, but always with

another Sister.

mise of fundamental importance: she must pray, because prayer fills

actions with the divine; she will be present...; the Superior, mother and guide, is always and

first of all in the praying community, a sign of unity and communion.

4 to be God's delight is, for the Mother, the beatitude that infinitely

surpasses every joy that can be tasted on earth.

5 One more recommendation, pressing and tightly reasoned: you have told

me and shown me by deeds that you love me; how happy I would be if you confirmed it

The teacher wants to go home; very well, have her read what the Mother writes here, then let her leave for Piacenza accompanied by a Sister. A replacement will be sent. She urges her to accept with courage whatever the Lord sends us.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I have just received your letter; I hear about the teacher;1 well then – listen, you will tell her that – or rather, you will read her these two lines.

2. Listen, you wish to go, and I will most willingly have you accompanied at once without delay; be so good as to leave on Monday morning, and as soon as you arrive here I will hand over your belongings, so that you can go home with no more crosses or fears. My daughter,

1. Here I am answering the two letters I have received from you since you have been in Rome; they were most welcome.1

2. You wish to know how to conduct yourself with the Children of Mary, whether you are to take Sr. A. Panasia's place. Yes, my daughter, you must do as she did; with regard to the Congregation you must not appear timid but all on fire for the Congregation of Mary, and encourage the members. You must do the same in the schools.2

How did he show himself pleased? Show yourself capable, docile; in short, the spirit of the Institute must be on your faces, is that not so, my daughter?4

an intense life of prayer and work, under the guidance of the dear Master Jesus

and directed towards attaining the love of God, to the point of being consumed in Him.

She informs her of the changes of Sisters to be made and already made. She confides her weariness and health difficulties. She finds comfort in Francesca's filial expressions and conduct.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received your letter and hear you complain that you have no letters from me. Listen, I have so much work that I have not a breath to spare, so overwhelmed am I; tomorrow Sr. A. Vincenza leaves, others left today; in short, I cannot find the time.1

2. Listen, you tell me you have sent the Sister to Sestri; you did well; it will be good for her to stay there. You see, today I sent them the Parmigiani girl, who wants to become a religious, and so she will do her year's training, and that Sister could study and teach with the girl.2

3. I hear that Sr. A. Enrichetta cannot hold out; so she can stay out of the classroom and just keep an eye on it from time to time, and then give lessons in the evening to Sr. A. Guglielma and the girl; so they will make progress, and it may be that this Sister takes to it and stays willingly, and Sr. A. Salvatore would be freed for me, for I need a Sister of long-standing vocation to send to a house that is to be opened.3

4. Try to pay a visit to Sestri. If you only knew: I sent Sr. A. Carmelina to S. P. d'Arena together with the girl, but I had told them to go to Genoa first; but once outside she said to the Sister: “I am going to S. P. d'Arena”. What heads, my God! See what she has done. She forgot the Superior's letter; I enclose it, send it on to her.4

5. One would need a thousand heads instead of one as small as mine, which always aches, for I think my brain is on the way to wearing out, because there is a real void in it and I feel the pain comes from its not being full enough; enough, let us leave it all.

6. Your letters are a real comfort to me; your words and your good conduct comfort me and assure me that I shall have my dear daughter with me for all eternity. Yes! you are too dear to me, so you must let me always have an anxious heartbeat for your good.

7. I commend the Sestri house to you; and listen to what I have written to the Superior. I want some religious removed from that house at S. P. d'Arena, because they seem to me too many. That nun you spoke to at Genoa, you did well; I had not sent her for you at all, I had sent her for Sestri; she is a complete goose.

Goodbye, your affectionate M. R.

1 tomorrow, 4 November, Sr. A. Vincenza leaves for Terricciola. Other Sisters have left for various destinations.

1 The Sister at Sestri: the one from Cortemaggiore, Sr. A. Guglielma Merli, cf. L 342,3; today I sent the Parmigiani girl (a young teacher) to Sestri, so that that Sister (Sr. A. Guglielma) could study and teach, helping the Parmigiani girl in class.

3 Sr. A. Enrichetta Salvatelli, the teacher, cannot hold out, stay in

the classroom for health reasons; so she can confine herself to supervising the school and

in the evening give lessons to the girl and Sr. A. Guglielma; it may be that the lat-

ter takes to it (giro) and stays willingly at Sestri; then I would transfer Sr.

A. Del Salvatore Orsi.

4 Try to visit the Sestri house now and then. I have transferred Sr. A. Car-

melina Carretta to the Sampierdarena Institute; she left with the girl (the Parmi-

giani girl). She forgot the letter of the Superior of Sestri, Sr. A. Giacomina Schenardi.

She has decided to send Sr. A. Maddalena for the school, but is still keeping her for now; meanwhile Carlotta can present the certificate to the Inspector. The Countess has asked for more religious and must be satisfied. She urges prudence about the things Carlotta asked for: she should be more precise and send a list of what is needed.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Listen carefully: I am sending you Sr. A. Maddalena, who has promised me to do well and not to cause you worry; moreover, being very good at her studies, she will do credit;2 meanwhile you will go to the Inspector with this certificate and the application, which I am sending you ready made out,3 and if you do not want to go you can send someone, but it is better that you go; and if he asks about the teacher, tell him she has to finish some business of her own and will soon be there; and if by chance he were to come, tell him she is at Piacenza on important business, and so you will be telling the truth. She is here, but you must know that I want to test her well first, because these teachers have heads that are frightening.

2. So do your best; the Countess has written to me that she sent you a sack of grain and wants me to increase the religious.4 Listen, the one I am sending you is very good, so she will be satisfied; meanwhile she will learn, and then, if you have too many, when I send you the teacher I will take them away; for now she must be satisfied.

3. Listen, when you write to me, try not to leave so much paper blank, but write from the top of the page as I do, because it is a fault against poverty.5 Handle the matter of the teacher well and

be careful to say nothing about Sr. A. Maddalena's not having a certificate; on the contrary, with the schoolgirls and with people outside and inside you must have her pass as certified, always without telling a lie. For charity's sake, keep everything well secret from those inside and outside. Do you understand? Be sure to say nothing to anyone.

4. You write asking me to send you things; my daughter, you know well

that we have no storehouses here, so you must specify

what you want and how much, of what quality, and for whom it is

needed, and then I will try to send you what you need.6 Be careful

not to give in too much: what is needed, yes; but you know well

that religious are leeches, and it would take far too much to satisfy

every wish. Send me a list and I will send you everything. I think

I have made myself clear.

Goodbye. The Lord bless you; and believe me always your

affectionate M. R.

5. I commend observance to you, and courage too. Cour-

age; take care of your health and pray, pray, my dear daugh-

ter, for with prayer everything will be obtained,

your affectionate M. R.

1 This letter was included in Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino's bundle, but

from its content and context it seems to be to Sr. A. Carlotta Biagini.

2 Having transferred the teacher, cf. L 341, she sends her Sr. A. Maddalena Ter-

zaghi, who, having a fair education (being good at her studies), will be able

to help run the school well.

3 You will go to the Inspector and hand him the certificate I am sending you (this one) and

the application; should he ask about the holder of the certificate, you will reply

that she is at Piacenza.

4 Countess Maria Anna Trotti; the one I am sending you: Sr. A. Maddalena.

5 not to leave paper blank. Sr. A. Carlotta had the habit of beginning her

letters a little over halfway down the page. This detail too confirms that she was

the addressee of the letter.

6 In her letter to the Mother of 31 October she had written: “the Sisters would

need dresses, bodices, drawers, and so I beg you to provide them”.

She sends him the documents for collecting the dowries of two novices. She gives him news of Sr. A. Vincenza's departure and work.

A.M.F. My Father,

1. Last night I received your letter and hear about the evil tongues, so zealous!1 I am sending you the papers; I hope you will be able to cash them and, God willing, you will then hand them to Sr. A. Domenica.2

2. Sr. A. Vincenza has left for Terricciola, and I have already had news that she was received with singing and enthusiasm; from there she will go on to S. Martinello for the 20th of this month, and I hope that for the Immaculate Conception she will spend two days at Foligno. I would like to tell you many more things, but I am alone and have an abyss of writing to do.

I am your

humble devoted Servant, Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 The evil tongues: “Monsignor (Negrotto), on his way to the Parrocchietta,

was telling me that those (the Sisters) at the Fornaci go short even of food, and

those with so much charity are, as usual, the Parish Priest and that Fr Giuseppe, who tell

Monsignor all the tittle-tattle”, so Fr Donadio on 5 November.

2 The papers: the documents he had dealt with for collecting the dowry of two

Sisters. (Cf. L 338, n. 1). He may cash them and hand the money to the Superior

Domenica Marchesini, Superior at the Fornaci.

She blesses the Lord on hearing that Vincenza is at Terricciola, and urges her to look after herself and not tire herself out. It would be good for her to go to the Bishop, now that she has time.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I am answering your last letter in haste, glad to hear that you have reached Terricciola; God be blessed.1 For charity's sake, take care of yourself. I am sorry to hear that you have stomach pains; mind, it is a bad sign; look after yourself, do not wear yourself out, for charity's sake.

2. I am well, and so is everyone; try to send me postulants, for I need them, soon.2 It is Saturday and we have no end of work. Goodbye; do not be upset if I write little, but time is too short.

Goodbye,

your affectionate M.

3. I am afraid you may have made a mistake in taking the Rules,

and instead of the ordinary ones have taken those for con-

fessors.3 If so, write to me at once and I will send them to you. It would be good

for you, while you are idle, to take the opportunity of going to the Bishop;4 so

you will receive a blessing for me, and you will thank him for the Pope's

blessing.

Goodbye; greet the Sisters for me.

1 your last, of 5 November.

2 try to send me postulants. “The archpriest is a man all

zeal and love for his parishioners; he is always in the confessional; every morning there are nearly fifty communions, almost all Children of Mary, with whom he takes such pains”... so Vincenza had written. The field is therefore well tilled, and the Mother sees it as fruitful in vocations for the Institute.

3 instead of the fundamental Rules; the others contained norms reserved

for confessors.

4 while you are idle: Sr. A. Vincenza had written to her: “we are still in the

archpriest's house, because in ours there is not yet a room free; the windows

are missing, everything is cluttered with masons”; take the opportunity of going to the Bish-

op (Mgr Ferdinando Capponi, Bishop of Volterra), the Mother suggests. (Cf.

L 359, n. 1). Sr. A. Vincenza went there on 10 November accompanied by the Archpriest

Secondo Griselli.

Various counsels on how to conduct herself in governing the community. She asks for prayers for a good outcome to the dispute with the Ricchini brothers.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am sending you two lines in reply for Sr. A. Perpetua's sister; read them to her, then have her write the address, and send it on to its destination.

2. I hear from your letter, which I received this morning, what Sr. A. Gerolama is doing. Listen, where Fr Accinelli is concerned you may let him act; you know he does everything for the good of the house; let her go to confession;1 and I am very glad that the Invorio Sisters are settling down; it gives me real pleasure.2

3. I commend the school to you; I hope soon to send you the printed book,3 and I am glad to hear that providence always comes to you.

4. Have some prayers said to Saint Anne to deliver me from taking the oaths. Have special prayers said in common every day to Our Lady of the Heart of Jesus too, for there is a suitable prayer, you know. For charity's sake, let them pray to this dear Virgin that I may be freed from such oaths. The sentence is coming soon; pray, pray, God can do everything. Ah, yes! may He convert these two unhappy priests once and for all.4

Goodbye, your affectionate M. R.

1 Sr. A. Gerolama Piralli had asked Fr Accinelli to write to her 644

relatives about financial matters concerning her. (L Fr Accinelli to M. Rosa, 18.10.74).

2 The Invorio postulants who had received the habit of the Daughters of Saint

Anne were being formed for religious life.

3 The school: practical lessons for the nurses, generally given, if pos-

sible daily, by the Superiors, using a special manual for the Daughters of

Saint Anne.

4 This is the Ricchini lawsuit, pursued not only by Angelo but also

by his brother Paolo. Cf. L 345, n. 6.

Apologizing for not being able to come in person, she asks his advice on how to proceed in the Ricchini case, since she is called upon to take oaths.

Your Most Reverend Excellency,

1. As I cannot come myself to humble myself at Your feet and seek advice on a most important matter, I must make use of the pen, sure that by this means too I shall receive the same answer from Your immense charity, of which I have had not a few proofs.

2. Your Excellency well knows that the Work of Saint Anne is engaged in a lawsuit,3 and now, after we have won it several times, the adversary, finding no other means, imposes oaths on me: either to swear or to return the money he gave me to open a house seven years ago,4 which still exists, full of girls and nuns, many of the girls having been placed there by the said priest and kept free of charge. Now I wish to know how I should proceed.

3. As I have only a few days in which to reply, for pity's sake, Your Excellency, do not leave me without an answer, which I await before making any decision. Grant me Your Pastoral Blessing; may it sustain me in such adversity.

[Your most humble Servant, Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO]

1 The autograph draft (MaM-10) lacks the addressee, who is deduced from the

content.

2 The date is deduced from the context. Cf. L 355,2; 357,4.

3 The Archbishop was very well informed. She herself had written to him on another

occasion, cf. L 141.

4 The house had been opened on 14 November 1868.

She returns the authorizations to him. She hopes he can collect the money and buy crucifixes for the novices who have none. He should have prayers said, for she is agitated about the oaths in the case with Fr Ricchini. She has accepted proposals to open houses at Mercatello, Mercatino, Ancona and Lugo. Sr. A. Vincenza is at Terricciola and will then be at Perugia.

A.M.F.

My Father,

1. I am sending you the two papers; who knows whether they will still be in order. Enough; if by good fortune the moment has come to receive the money, with fifty of it buy me as many crucifixes as usual for the religious, for I have now clothed a good batch,1 but they have no crucifix and keep asking me whether Father Agostino has written to say he is sending them, because I told them I would write to you to get them; but first I wanted to hear whether you had received these religious' money.

2. My Father, in a few days they are to hear the Ricchini case;2 have some prayers said to St Francis, that he may go with his staff. What a weight of pain I bear! You cannot believe it; I feel constantly agitated at the thought of the oaths. Perhaps they will hear it in 10 or 15 days; tell the Sisters to pray, and all the good souls you know.

4. I have settled on three more houses: one at Mercatello, another at Mercatino, and also at Ancona, whose Cardinal wrote me a most beautiful letter; and I have settled Lugo too.3

5. You will know that Sr. A. Vincenza is at Terricciola, and by the twentieth

she will be at Perugia.4 If she does not arrive in time for the date I have fixed for these other houses, then I shall go myself. The Mercatello house is in the diocese of Pesaro, and I go there willingly because it is a good municipality, the negotiations having been conducted together with the Curia. I say nothing of my health, because I can tell you nothing good; I am very poorly, especially my head.

Your poorest Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 I am sending you: cf. L 351, n. 2. Who knows whether the documents will still be valid, but

if he collects the money, let him spend 50 F on the usual crucifixes for the religious, for I have clothed

a good number...

2 The Ricchini case, cf. L 354. Tell the Sisters to pray. She too has

asked and keeps asking for special prayers, cf. L 353,4; 345, n. 6; 357,4. L 376,4.

3 Mercatello, cf. L 356; Mercatino Conca (L 374), Ancona, L 336,1, Lugo di

Ravenna, L 346.

4 She had told him so on 7 November (cf. L 351,2).

She is glad to learn of the Town Council's favourable decision concerning the Sisters' coming. She puts forward some points: the addition of a fourth Sister and premises with the bare essentials, and she asks for the date of the Sisters' arrival.

[Reverend Archpriest],

1. I am replying to your most esteemed letter, which I have the pleasure of receiving today, the 12th of this month. I am delighted to hear that the Most Honourable Council has welcomed my letter and that all is well for arranging our arrival.

2. Now allow me first to make an observation which seems to me most just and which Your Most Reverend Lordship will no doubt admit. Since the three Sisters must be continuously occupied with the three schools,1 a fourth seems to me absolutely necessary, to prepare a little dinner for them and do whatever is needed in their small dwelling, as we have no servants nor can we keep any.

3. Do not trouble yourself too much about our dwelling, for we are accustomed to make do with bare necessities, such as: a table for meals, the necessary chairs, a wardrobe for the linen, a writing table. As for the premises: if the rooms are large enough for three or four to sleep in, the beds must have curtains; a small parlour with chairs only; a room for meals; the kitchen with the necessary utensils, and plain linen, yes, but new.

4. I would like you to indicate roughly when – if you decide to proceed – I should send them, since I also have to open another house in this neighbourhood.2 I forgot to tell you that the journey must be at your expense. In the sweet hope that the poor Daughters

of Saint Anne will be able to offer their Work in your Town, deign to bless me, while I have the honour to sign myself Your Reverend Lordship's

most humble Servant, Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 the three Sisters continuously occupied with the three schools: constantly engaged

in the three classes...

2 another nearby: at Mercatino Conca, also in the province of Urbino,

like Mercatello.

She is worried by Vincenza's silence. In her own way of life all is proceeding with order and perfect observance. She has accepted a house at Mercatello and another at Mercatino. She asks for fervent prayers for the “Ricchini lawsuit”.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line to you first, as soon as I sat down at my desk;1 for two days I have had no letters from you, and it makes me anxious; I fear for your health; I assure you it is a great worry to me; for charity's sake, take care of yourself.

2. In my examination last night I found that it did not please the Lord at all that both you and Sr. A. Francesca kept up a way of life with me such as staying on in the evening;2 you cannot believe how much more observant I find myself now that I do not stay up at all, and so I keep silence all day; in the evening, after the rosary, I shut myself in my room. If I have writing to do I stay in the study, but alone and in silence; and in the morning I do my best to get up early.

3. Everything is going in good order; I have accepted another house at Urbino, that is, from Urbino for Mercatello, and another at Mercatino; who knows, I may come and join you.3

4. Listen, have some prayers said for the lawsuit; it will be heard within days, and your uncle has replied to you saying that I shall certainly have to take the oaths; but God can do everything, and prayer moves mountains. For charity's sake, commend me to the good and devout young women, for I promise you a month of communions for this grace;

you form the intention well; I am writing everywhere for prayers. Ah, my God, what pain!4

5. You will have received my letter; the post has just come and there are no letters from you; for charity's sake, do what you can. I add nothing more, because I have so much work. Goodbye,

your affectionate M.

God bless you, and believe me yours for all ages.

1 A line to you first: before anyone else, as soon as she is at her desk.

2 Reviewing her life before the Lord the previous evening, she found

that He was not pleased with Francesca's and Vincenza's settled habit of

staying on in the evening to talk with her... Now I find myself much more observant of the strict

silence prescribed by the Rule.

3 If both places send for them soon, she may go herself and

join her.

4 Cf. L 355, n. 2.

She knows the cause of Carlotta's trouble and so invites her to come to her. She expects her at once, grieved to know she is suffering. She herself cannot move because of work and poor health. She awaits her. Let her promise Jesus that she will obey, leave, pour out her heart to her Mother and be consoled by her.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I understand where your trouble comes from; listen, you would give me a great present if you could come over here to me; I have so many things to tell you, lovely ones, not ugly ones, which will be a real consolation to you; and meanwhile you will take the teacher and bring me the Sister.1

2. Come, my dear daughter, leaning on obedience; come, and you will be completely healed and able to take up your work again for the glory of God and the good of your neighbour. I expect you at once, do not delay; I will give you the money for the journey; I am waiting for you. Carlotta, all mine for eternity, you certainly do not know how dear you are to me, and hearing you are unwell grieves me too much.2 Had I not seen lines from you on the back of one from Sr. A. Maddalena, I would have come at once.3

3. My dear daughter, if you knew how worn out I am with work! Sr. A. Vincenza is away, so I have the whole burden of the desk and the letters; I always have a bad headache, and besides we have so many houses to open, so I must prepare the Sisters.4

4. Goodbye, I am waiting for you. Say to dear Jesus: “I want to obey, and I want to go to my Mother and pour out my heart; she meanwhile will console me”. Leave Sr. A. Costantina as

Superior, that is, in your place, for 24 hours. Tell them to say nothing, because nothing can happen in twenty-four hours. Yours for all ages,

affectionately, MOTHER R.

1 I understand where your trouble comes from. Not having received letters from the Mo-

ther, she had lost heart: “I wish to know whether you are displeased with me... and whether you still

consider me your daughter, because from this silence I foresee that there is something

amiss”, so on 12.11.74.

2 The Mother finds the healing remedy at once: come... leaning on obe-

dience (because she felt unwell)... I expect you at once. She thus calms her fears even be-

fore embracing and consoling her. Feeling unwell: Carlotta had written to her:

“God will know why He keeps me so oppressed and pierced”.

3 Had I not received the letter in your own hand after Sr. A.

Maddalena's, I would have come to you.

4 Sr. A. Vincenza is away; we have houses to open. Cf. L 355,4-5.

She tells her the day on which the Sisters are to meet her at Florence station to go to Perugia. She will then go to Foligno. She suggests what Vincenza should write to her uncle about their work and the “Ricchini lawsuit”.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I have just received your letter and hear how well you were received by the good bishop.1 My God, when our Superiors receive us well, everything is blessed by God!

2. I hope to send the Superior to Foligno on Monday or Wednesday, so you can write to me and to the Superior Sr. A. Eufemia the time and day on which we, that is the Sisters, are to meet: I must have them meet at Florence, and Sr. A. Eufemia must go on to Perugia, do you understand?2 I would think Thursday the 19th of this month best, since the twentieth falls on a Friday and you have no time to stay; only two days will be too few.

3. Perhaps Sr. A. Eufemia will be accompanied by Signora Maria, who can then serve you very well for the return journey to Foligno, for I long for you to go there;3 and at Foligno do not forget that money: have notice given, otherwise the term will expire and it cannot be collected. I hope you have taken the two hundred francs, and a few others besides.4 Have Mancini's postulants not arrived after all?5

4. How much work there is at this desk! Today my hand hurt so much that I had to rub it with that water in order to go on.6 How dear your letters were to me!

5. Listen, write a little to your uncle, thank him for the letter he

wrote you and tell him you are travelling about, setting up houses, and give him the number 26, which is true, since they have been settled; that we shall certainly meet at Lugo or Pesaro; you can tell him that we are one in one place and one in another, so great is the crowd of requests; and this only so that it may be of use to him for the hearing, which will be in a few days; today the two lawyers held a conference to prepare.7 Write to him at once and tell him always to address your letters to Piacenza, and that you will be very glad if he keeps you informed.

6. So we are agreed that on Thursday the 19th of this month I shall have the religious leave at 11 at night, so as to be in Florence in the morning at half past 7,8 a.m.

Goodbye. The Lord bless you and everyone; your

affectionate M. R.

1 The letter is dated 11 November and speaks at length of the welcome given by the

Bishop of Volterra, Mgr Ferdinando Capponi.

2 on which we are to meet, or rather the Sisters are to meet at Florence,

and Sr. A. Eufemia Camporesi is to go to Perugia.

3 Perhaps she will be accompanied by Signora Maria Grampini, who will be able

to keep you company on your journey to Foligno.

4 I hope you have taken, have brought with you, the 200 F. They had been given by the father

of a postulant from Peccioli, Vincenza had written to her.

5 Fr Mancini: cf. L 315,8. He had already presented several postulants.

6 my hand hurt: cf. L 316, n. 5.

7 The uncle, the lawyer Domenico Boccardo, was defending the Mother in the Ricchini case.

You will tell him that our houses are 26 (the number 26), which is true, agreements having already

been made for other foundations; and that we shall certainly meet at

Lugo and Pesaro; ...so great is the number (the crowd) of requests; you will say this only

so that it may serve him for the defence, that is, as proof of the Institute's solidity

to be presented in the court proceedings. Today the two lawyers met

(Boccardo and Debernardis) to prepare, to reach an understanding.

8 At 7.30.

This letter will be handed to her by the teacher, an excellent person, replacing the other Sister, whom she is to send away. She advises her how to deal with a lady who wants to meddle in the affairs of the house.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. You will receive this letter from the teacher; she will direct the school; I commend her to you; you understand me: she likes to be made a little fuss of;2 leave the other two who are there, put the one who is with them among the boarders, and remove Luigia at once, for I am uneasy since she told me she knows so many ugly things. Meanwhile, this one is very good and you will be very pleased; and at the first opportunity send Luigia here; meanwhile keep an eye on her and forbid her to speak with the others, especially these new ones.3

2. How is providence? And your health? This teacher will be a great relief to you and you will be able to take counsel with her. For charity's sake, try by your good way of acting – I hope you will see that she becomes wholly Saint Anne's.4 Goodbye, your

affectionate [MOTHER]

3. Write and tell me you are well. Listen, go with her to the Inspector to put yourselves in order.5

4. You write that Signora Maria has written you certain things that upset you.6 Pay no heed to any of it; we are not obliged to answer anonymous letters; it means they are people who cannot

show their faces. So take no notice; if she writes to you again and puts her address, then reply to her in black ink, saying that you beg her to remain the lay person she is and not to meddle in matters that are no concern of hers, since you have your superiors and are in no way bound to accept corrections from her. Let her beware of doing so, being a poor lay person who does not know what religion means.7 I hope she will write no more such things to you. Goodbye, your

affectionate M. R.

1 This letter, although dated, was included in the undated bundle of Sr. A.

Vincenza Rapallino. It is clearly addressed to Sr. A. Carlotta Biagini.

2 from the teacher. This is Sr. A. Onorata Casati; she wants to be treated lov-

ingly (made a fuss of).

3 You will transfer (remove) Sr. A. Luigia, because she knows of matters that could

circulate among the Sisters and give scandal, especially to the newcomers.

4 wholly Saint Anne's. Sr. A. Onorata had received the religious habit on 29 Sep-

tember 1874, so she was to be formed in the spirit of the Institute.

5 with her... in order. Present the young woman and the necessary docu-

ments to the school Inspector for authorization to teach.

6 In her letter (of 14.11.74) Sr. A. Carlotta had written to her: “I have received a letter

from Signora Maria, who reproaches me a great deal and among other things tells me to

be kind and treat the Sisters and pupils with love... she wrote me an anonymous

letter”.

7 To remain a lay person: that is, to act as an outsider and not meddle in

matters that do not concern her. She does not know, cannot understand, the spirit that animates

religious life.

She has received a letter from the Marchioness Spinola, who has promised to pay the subsidy for this month. Vincenza is to ask her to give her opinion of the Religious. The Mother has written to the Duchess proposing to close the elementary school and keep only the home nursing and, if needed, the sewing school for the older girls. Vincenza is to see what should be done. But she must insist that catechism be taught in church every Sunday and that enclosure be observed, with no outsiders allowed into the Sisters' rooms.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. You will receive this from the hands of Sr. A. Eufemia. First of all, the Marchioness has written to me saying that as soon as you arrive she will give you fr. 50 for the month of November, although it is already begun and well advanced, and that you will find everything else, so she tells me.2 Tell her that if she is not satisfied with any of the religious she should write to me and we will make an exchange at once; and likewise, if anything is not to her liking, she should tell me frankly, for I will try to satisfy her in everything.

2. Meanwhile, listen: I am writing to Signora Maria to try to accompany Sr. A. Eufemia to Perugia, and then she would serve you for your own return; enough; I sense clearly, as I write, that this weighs on you and you do not like it, so I trust in the Lord that Sr. A. Eufemia will manage well and travel by day, and so nothing will happen.3 Meanwhile, for charity's sake, write to me as soon as you arrive.

3. When you go to Foligno you will look into things; first of all you will write to the Inspector that Sr. A. Carmelina is no longer at Foligno and had to leave for reasons of health, and tell him that if the schools continue another teacher will be provided,4 for you must know that I have written to the Duchess that I would be in favour of giving up the academic school altogether and keeping, if there are older girls who want to come and sew, that, and for the rest having nurses as at Genoa, which seems much better to me; moreover it is clear that this work is far dearer to the town than the schools; and besides, you can understand that I do not know how to manage, having so many houses to open.5 Ah, if it could be arranged, how good it would be to succeed in this!

4. Listen, I heard from Sr. A. Eufemia that catechism was no longer even being taught in Church; tell Sr. A. Giovannina never to give it up; you will see to it.6

5. Horror! I hear that all the secular priests used to go into the sick Sisters' room, even the D...'s maids. Find out more and put things in order. Signora Maria, though, will have to be allowed in, for I hear it would cause too much of a stir, as she is a benefactress and so used to it. You will see to everything properly; and let the two sick Sisters be together.

6. Dear daughter, what a horror! The accounts for the clothings: one is a thousand 149 and the other 900; what do you say? I paid the blacksmith, and it was 79. In short, that is all we do, my God! Make sure you can collect the Tuzzi money;8 at S. Martinello be quick, so that you can stay a little longer at Foligno.

Goodbye, all [yours] for all ages,

affectionately, M.
