She urges them not to worry about their Superior: there is nothing serious, she no longer has a fever and will soon be back among them. Meanwhile they are to be prudent, obedient and silent, and to pray much.

A.M.F.

My daughters,

1. I heard from Sr. A. Benedetta how upset you all are about your Superior.1 Be at peace, for it is nothing; it was all gossip, misunderstandings and nothing more; God's permission, for He wishes to test us so; but courage.

2. Let us learn from Peter, the Saviour's successor, not to flee from suffering but rather to work courageously in the way of the Lord.2

3. I want you to say nothing more about anything among yourselves; rumours spread, and the tongue is a knife that cuts with seven blades.3 For charity's sake, silence; in a few days your Superior will be with you – I mean the Superior, Sr. A. Carlotta. Since yesterday she has had no fever and is beginning to be better; so be at peace; pray hard to the good God for me.

4. I want all your conversation to be holy, and your actions too. Obey; I shall soon be with you. Goodbye. The Lord bless you; and believe me always your poor

M. ROSA

1 She has heard from Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega that they are worried about their Supe-

rior. She, accepting the Mother's invitation (cf. L 358,2), had gone to Piacen-

za to her.

2 Let us learn from Peter to follow the Saviour and work courageously

(Mt 5:18-19).

3 I want you not to talk about it, because the tongue can do so much harm.

“If anyone thinks he is religious and does not bridle his tongue... his religion

is vain” (Jas 1:26).

She will send him the two certificates. For the opening of the Hospital she will provide a Superior skilled in surgery and dentistry.

[Reverend Archpriest]

1. I thank you infinitely for your most esteemed letter, which I have the honour of receiving today, the 19th of this month. How obliged I am to you for the trouble you took for us in preference to other, better Institutes! Everything is settled; within eight days Your Reverend Lordship will have the two certificates.1

2. I intend to send you a capable Superior, also for the opening of the hospital,2 already experienced, and she will be able at once, if you wish, to put into practice that charity, for in the hospital where she now serves as assistant she is used to the school of surgery, her duties including pulling teeth. I will try to provide her with her instruments,3 so that she may be of use to poor humanity.

With a thousand respects to the Honourable Council, and begging Your Most Reverend Lordship to bless me, I remain with all esteem and veneration

your most humble and devoted Servant, Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 The letter is dated 16 November. Everything is settled: as to the number

of Sisters, four and not three (cf. L 356,2), and the annual payment for each

(L 350), as proposed to her.

2 also for the opening of the hospital: the new community was to take on,

besides the girls' school, the running of the small hospital. (Cf. L of Fra Paci-

fico Sampaolesi, 9 November 1874, AFSA, FcIC).

3 with the necessary instruments.

She has heard that Francesca is ill and is greatly distressed at the thought that she herself was the cause, having sent her to the station on foot. She will have prayers said for her. She need not worry about Sr. A. Carlotta: she is content and steadfast.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter Francesca, all mine,

1. For pity's sake take care of yourself; ah, do not kill me; hearing that you are ill is more painful to me than everything else.1 God will see to it; the Sisters have arrived and I learned it only now, at 8 in the morning.2 I was in anguish all night, because I kept thinking of you being ill.

2. Today a triduum to the Eternal Father begins for your healing. Alas, I feel my heart bursting, my Francesca; I made a grave mistake, which has cost me tears to think of: I sent you to the station on foot. Oh, what a horror, and you must have suffered.3 Ah, forgive me, for pity's sake! Perhaps that is what brought on the blood.4 So look after yourself.

3. You tell me to send her things.5 Never again; everything has been settled. Sr. A. Carlotta is still steadfast and content; those who came to fetch her have already gone home satisfied.6 For the rest I shall write to you at greater length.

4. This evening I am [sending this] so that it reaches you. Rest easy, everything is settled and in order. The battles are dying down. Go ahead according to your own judgement, without waiting for my orders. Do what God inspires you, and I approve and bless everything.

Yours affectionately for all ages,

M. R.

1 take care of yourself... everything else. Her poor state of health is more painful to her

than the unpleasant events in the Sampierdarena community: the flight of the Supe-

rior Augusta and of Sr. A. Tecla Mazzini, and the resulting unrest in the community.

Sr. A. Francesca had had to hurry there to assess the situation and

apply the remedies needed for good order. She had therefore had to talk, clarify,

calm people down and send some Sisters off to Piacenza.

2 The transferred Sisters had arrived in the evening.

3 I sent you to the station. She had asked her to accompany per-

sonally the above-mentioned Sisters to the station.

4 This must have caused the haemoptysis.

5 To send her things to Sr. A. Augusta.

6 Sr. A. Carlotta (Augusta's sister) is steadfast; the family members who

had come to persuade her to go with them for treatment had left

satisfied.

She denounces the grave injustice of the discriminatory pay between the resident girls and the outside workers and gives notice that she will withdraw hers unless it is remedied.

Most Illustrious Signor Emilio Poss,

1. I deeply regret having to tell you that I cannot continue to leave some 70 girls working in your factory for such low wages, while the outside workers receive eighty centesimi each and we the miserable sum of 20 or 25 centesimi, and one or two forty.1

2. Think it over: if at the end of the month, the first of December, if at the end or the beginning of that month I do not have an increase, I am resolved to withdraw them.2

Please accept my sentiments of respect and esteem.

Your most humble Servant, Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 the outside workers were paid more; they had been pre-

sented by, and were thus protected by, the Prefecture of Piacenza.

2 Think it over. She is precise and peremptory. She means: if the increase is not

paid in advance, on 1 December or at the end of that month, she will withdraw the

girls.

She has not written sooner because she was waiting for the teacher to leave so as to send what Carlotta asked for; that is the only reason, not any lack of affection. She warns her about a Sister's way of behaving towards Superiors. Other instructions and news.

My daughter,

1. I have just finished reading your two lines and am answering at once, though my head is bandaged because of the pain. What a consolation it was to hear you are better! You complain that I do not write to you. My dear, you know, the reason is this: every day I thought I would be able to tell you that the teacher is coming; and my affection for my dear daughter is too great. Who put such ugly thoughts into your head? For charity's sake, never let it be!

2. Listen, I forgot to tell you to take care not to let yourself be ensnared by the Sister I sent you,2 because she always did this with every Superior, and she is very deceitful. For charity's sake, watch her and keep her in her place like the others.

3. Listen, the religious teacher I have is not suitable for Ferrara, and I am obliged to send you a lay one.3 I hear what you tell me about the Sister; well, look, I shall withdraw her; you know well that journeys cost money, and this year they are no small expense for me.4 Enough; if Sr. A. Rosa can no longer stay there, you can get the doctor to make out a certificate like the other one you sent me, so that I can tell the Countess I withdrew her on the doctor's orders.5

4. Then they can come together, and next Wednesday I shall send you the teacher, and through those who are to come you will send me back the certificate I sent you and renew the application in the name of the one who will arrive.

5. For the rest, I have already prepared the caps, drawers and bodices; only I am surprised that Sr. A. Maddalena still wants things, for she took more than her share; and besides, she knows the rules: she is not to know whether she has three or four, but it is enough that she always has everything she needs on Saturday. Keep her in check, for charity's sake.6

6. Dear daughter, take care of yourself, and when you have more means, or at least no debts, you can slip away into my arms; I await you, and sign myself

your affectionate M. R... God bless you, and I am yours, M...

1 This letter was classified among those to Sr. A. Vincenza Ra-

pallino, but is in fact to Sr. A. Carlotta Biagini: cf. L 350, n. 1.

2 not to let yourself be ensnared, cunningly won over, by the Sister I

sent you (perhaps Sr. A. Maddalena, cf. L 350,1).

3 a lay one: a lay teacher.

4 I hear what you tell me: in the letter of 19.11 she is answering, Carlotta had written: “Sr.

A. Onorata is cold and knows nothing... she is sad and says one cannot live here”.

The Mother is of the opinion that she should be withdrawn.

5 if Sr. A. Rosa can no longer stay. M. Rosa had already decided on her trans-

fer, but had had to give it up because of the opposition of Countess Maria Anna

Trotti. (Cf. L 319,3).

6 The things she has prepared had been asked for by the Superior: cf. L 350,

n. 6. She warns her, however, against the demands of Sr. A. Maddalena, who has

learned the Institute's customs and knows well that she is not to know how many pieces of

linen she has, and must be content to be given what she normally

needs; keep her in her place, for charity's sake.

She is deeply distressed to hear that Francesca is ill and begs her to take care of herself. As soon as she is well she is to take eight days' leave and come to Piacenza. She need not worry about the Sister, who seems repentant. She is to send the things left behind by the other two.

A.M.F.

My daughter, dear to me for all ages,

1. Ah, the pain of hearing you are ill [is great]! I am telegraphing you now; everyone tells me no, there will be letters today. For pity's sake, have someone write to me; do not fret, rest in bed, do not worry; in short, whatever is needed, spare nothing. As soon as you are well, take a little leave for 8 days, and come and rest a while and stay with me.2

2. Think no more of those unhappy women, for I already see them very repentant.3 Sr. A. Carmelina weeps and despairs because I have pronounced sentence on her, and she sends word and told me herself to give her whatever penance I wish, that she is ready to do it, and that she has wronged me badly. She says that not everything Fr Accinelli said is true; in short, it was the devil who made her do it.4 There you are: when they no longer know what to say, they say it was the devil, when they know a trick more than he does. Horrible infamy! Can more be said? To kiss Jesus and then betray him!

3. Oh, dear daughter, how much good this meditation on Judas does me! [When] I am upset and cannot find much recollection, I pass at once to this point, and I assure you that I soon find myself so with my God in His sorrow that I cannot help weeping.

4. As for the things, tell the Superior to send me everything left by those two unhappy women, and also those of Sr. A. Pastore, you know; she has to be changed often.5

Goodbye, for I have too much work. Sr. A. Carlotta sends you warm greetings and longs to see you as I do; so we shall tell you many more things in person;6 but no one can be as devoted to you as I am; yours eternally,

M. R.

2 Cf. L 364,1-2.

the two unhappy women: Augusta Biagini and Tecla Mazzini, who had left the Sampierdarena Institute without permission, taking money and gold objects with them. (Cf. L 364, n. 1).

4 Sr. A. Carmelina Carretta knew of the intentions of the two unhappy

women; not only that: she had told Fr Accinelli she wanted to “leave the convent”.

(L Accinelli to M. Rosa, 18.11.74). Now she is at Piacenza, weeping and despairing.

5 Tell the Superior who replaced Augusta, Sr. A. Elisabetta Veronesi,

to send me the things left by those unhappy women and those of Sr. A. Del Buon Pastore

Most Illustrious Congregation,

1. Having received your most esteemed letter requesting four Sisters for the Schools under your direction, and after negotiation having agreed a stipend of 1,200 francs and premises entirely free of any other occupant: these conditions being accepted by both parties, the matter is concluded by a letter of reply from you telling me when the Sisters are to come.

She tells her of the arrival of the postulant teacher and asks her to speak to the Superior about her, commending her.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A couple of lines in haste to tell you that tomorrow, on the 4 p.m. train, the teacher for the house1 arrives and will come to the hospital, so have her accompanied. I like her very much; she is with her mother and will stay until Sunday, that is, Monday, and then she will come back here alone.

2. For charity's sake, take care of yourself; and soon, that is, we shall see each other; I long for it. Ask the Superior to be considerate to her; let them put her in the refectory with them. Let the food be the same, good as it ought to be for all. For her, two things: a little wine; I hope Sr. A. Elisabetta2 will grow fond of her, and it will be a great good for the house. She is very shy; she needs to be helped to get over it a little.3 Goodbye, I want to post this,

your affectionate M. I shall write to you again through her.4

1 the teacher for the house arrives, that is, for the Institute. She is presumed to be the postulant,

because she asks that she be given her meals in the refectory with the Sisters.

2 Sr. Elisabetta is the Superior.

3 She is very shy; she needs to become more at ease (get over) her shy-

ness.

4 She will send her a letter through the young woman mentioned above. It is L 371.

She informs her of the teacher's arrival and entrusts her to her care. She advises her to put the house back in order, paying the debts and treating the Sisters well.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am sending you the teacher and I hope she will do well; she is very good and has a splendid certificate; keep an eye on her, and give her the same food as yourselves, good milky coffee, and you can put her in your refectory; she is no trouble at all.1

2. I have received your letter; it was very dear to me. Yes, my daughter, wretched creatures, who knows where they will end up; I do not know.2 Let us pray for them, that God may give them the grace of perseverance in their vocation.

3. Listen, for charity's sake, keep a close watch on those two vipers you have in that house, lest they too start scheming; what thieving, my God!3

4. I hear about the bills they left; it is horrifying; see, for charity's sake, whether you can pay some off with the fees; I also urge you to see that the bread, maize and pasta can be paid for out of the fee money, as we had reckoned.4

5. I say no more, for I know how capable you are at economizing; so let the religious eat and drink, but let them suffer no more; the ingenious woman manages [everything], with work, with begging.5 Enough; I hope I shall have consolations and see that poor house flourish again. I am sure of it. Goodbye; the Lord bless you; and believe me always your affectionate

M. R.

1 Cf. L 369,2.

2 wretched creatures. The two Sisters who fled the House. Cf. L 367, n. 3.

3 those two vipers: so the two Vernengo sisters were called. Cf. L 206,

n. 5; che ladronissi is Genoese: latronizzii = thefts.

4 I hear about the debts left by the two mentioned above, n. 2. If you could

pay them off with the girls' fees, and also buy the bread, maize and

pasta, as we had reckoned.

5 begging was one of the means of support.

She is always taken up with many things and has had to contend with certain people. The enemy is at work, but she hopes soon to see him put to shame. Francesca should encourage Sr. A. Elisabetta to be a strong woman and not run up large debts.

A.M.F. My Francesca,

1. Today I wrote to tell you that the teacher would be arriving. She brings you this letter of mine;1 it is odd that I wrote to you and then did not notice that I was speaking to the Superior of the house, telling her what she had to do, how she was to treat this young woman arriving with them. What will you have said?2

2. You see, there are so many things, and such things, that I must attend to, that I really do not know which way to turn to fulfil my obligations; dear Francesca, I hope the moment will soon come when I can talk to you.

3. Oh, how much I have to tell you! Today I had a long battle with Ci in... and Maddalena. I am also at odds with Bologna;3 in short, Cifone is putting on a show behind my back, but I hope soon to break his horns and see him roasting under a pot. Enough. Stabs from every side, but I hope it will rebound on his own Cifo.4

4. Encourage Sr. A. Elisabetta; tell her to act as a strong and invincible woman, fearing no one; strong.5 I commend the accounts to you: let her not run up large ones. What a martyrdom this moment is, under so many expenses! Goodbye (yours); greet the Sisters for me.

God bless them, and you in particular, while I am yours for eternity.

Affectionately and closely, M. R.

1 This letter of mine: she had announced it in L 269.

2 I was speaking to the Superior of the house: some of the instructions did not in fact

concern Francesca directly.

3 long battle with Ci in... and Maddalena. Presumably Canon Insani

and Maddalena Parmigiani, over the Cortemaggiore house. As for Bologna,

that is, Countess Trotti, cf. L 373,1.

4 Cifone: a derogatory name, hideous face; cifo, ugly snout. She expresses

a firm will to oppose evil in whatever form it appears.

5 Sr. Elisabetta, the Superior who must repair the damage done by her

predecessor.

She advises her to provide the Sisters with overcoats and the clothing needed to keep out the cold. She is to be diligent in requiring reports on the care of the sick and prudent about what she comes to know. She is to watch over everything carefully.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received all your letters, including the last, in which you told me you are putting something aside. I would like you also to think of clothing the religious and having an overcoat made for each, because I see it is very necessary and it is good that all should have one; and also drawers and woollen bodices, which will protect them well from catching aches, stitches and coughs. I hope you will do it in the same way as you did the mattresses.1

2. I also want you to be more diligent in receiving the reports, not to risk sending the same two Sisters together too often, and to be prudent, not revealing the Sister who has told you of her companion's fault.2

3. I do not know why, but for two days I have had a great fear about the Genoa house; I am afraid there is some disorder; in short, keep watch night and day if you want to do what God commands you through your Superiors.

4. Try to go and visit the sick whom the Sisters are nursing.3

5. As for that gentleman who wants to know about Sr. A. Vincenza and the air, I do not know what to tell him, because I do not understand such things; let him ask the doctor, who will tell him something.4

Greet the Sisters for me, and believe me your

affectionate M. God bless you

1 In her last letter (of 25.11) Sr. A. Santina gives her good news about

the essential expenses for the house, including the mattresses.

2 The Sisters, who always went in pairs to nurse the sick at home,

were to report to the Superior. The Mother advises her to receive these re-

ports more diligently. She should also try to avoid sending the same two Sisters

together to the sick too often. And further: let her be prudent and not re-

veal the faults of one of the two Sisters which the other may have disclosed to her.

3 It is good for her to go in person to see the sick and the service

given by the Sisters.

4 As for that gentleman. A lawyer – writes the Superior – had learned

from Sr. A. Vincenza's sister that she suffered from asthma and that the air of Piacenza had

done her so much good that she was cured. He wants more precise information about it, because

his wife suffers from the same complaint.

.

She writes to Foligno telling Vincenza to inform Countess Trotti on her way back, as the Countess is annoyed that she did not call on her. She will send Sr. A. Filomena to Ferrara with the teacher. She wants Vincenza to stop at least two days at Ferrara to put everything in good order. She herself is in the most dreadful tribulations.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I hope this finds you at Foligno, where I am addressing it. Listen, when you return, be sure to notify Countess Trotti.1 My dear, if you knew how much trouble she has given me! She even telegraphed me that you had already gone through; in short, you cannot imagine how many things were invented; and she sent Signora Teresa,2 and I will not tell you how much she said to me on the Countess's orders, a thousand silly things. Enough, all for God.

2. You must know that tomorrow I am sending Sr. A. Filomena with the teacher, who wants to try for a year and is a lay person, since I did not want to clothe her.3 I have had all these things written to the Countess.

3. Sr. A. Giovannina4 wrote to me that the doctor has prescribed steam baths for the Sister and that a man is needed to load the apparatus; very well, the man yes, but the nuns no, I do not want them to come. You will certainly be firmer than I am.5

4. I shall not write to you here any more; I shall write to you at Ferrara, where I want you to stop for two days to see everything and put it all in good order. I have received yours and was glad to hear so much good news amid the most dreadful tribulations, which are suffocating me; I am

at the height, one might say an abyss; I do not know where my head is.

Goodbye, dear Vincenza, I long to embrace you. Believe me, in the depths of sorrow, yours for all ages.

Goodbye, affectionately, M.

1 be sure to notify, inform.

2 Signora Teresa Zagotti, her secretary.

3 Tomorrow I am sending Sr. A. Filomena Pugnaloni to Ferrara to accom-

pany the teacher. She is still a lay person, because she has not been allowed to receive the reli-

gious habit.

4 Sr. A. Giovannina Pizzorno, the Superior of the Foligno house; the steam

baths for the sick Sister.

5 You will be firmer than I in having my wishes observed.

She cannot accept his request, since it is the Institute's practice to found houses with no fewer than four Sisters. She says she is willing to oblige him, but with the stated number.

Most Illustrious Sir,

1. I regret that I cannot accept your request, for the reason that we cannot go fewer than four; I am therefore sorry to have to withdraw, awaiting the renewed expression of your wish.1

2. Should you be unable to do without for your Schools, do not hesitate to apply again, for we shall always be ready to come, with the number I have stated.2

Please accept the sentiments of deep esteem of one who professes herself yours, Most Illustrious Sir,

[ROSA GATTORNO]

1 For other requests for teaching Sisters too she had kept

firmly to this number.

2 She leaves the door open, while remaining firm in her requirement.

She confesses that she is at the height of her tribulations and tries to bear everything with love. One must be patient and not lose heart. In the end death comes and seals everything; sweet is the thought of going to Jesus' feet and entering his Kingdom without waiting in antechambers, having waited in so many in this world. She commends a Sister to her.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. A line to tell you that Fr...A... has been here; how an-g... he was because you took the Sister! He told me you had asked him to send her to you; is it true? Try to smooth things over so that he is not offended, for these are dreadful times for us.1 God wishes to humble us, and I assure you I am now carrying a good load of it; if the good God helps me to bear everything for His love in holy resignation, for the flesh writhes under so cruel a martyrdom2 that never ends, nor can one tell when it will end. Patience!

2. Take care of yourself, do not be disheartened, for in the end death comes and everything is over; it seals every sorrow, and we are left with the sweet thought of bringing it to Jesus' feet in payment for our sins and of being able to enter his kingdom without having to wait in the antechamber, having waited in so many in this world at the doors of the gentry – what cold we suffered, what humiliations;3 in short, it seems to me that antechambers are very painful; and the one that would keep us from entering quickly to embrace the One we so love would be too painful.

3. I have left Fr Accinelli F. 1,500 to pay the debts of

S. P. d'Arena; he has received a postulant and is sending her to me here.4 I urge you to keep a close watch on Sr. A. Domitilla, because her silence, her refusal to say anything, is very alarming; it means she is deeply implicated; and, enough, I commend her to you.5

Goodbye, my dear daughter; tell me, when will you come? I am yours for ever,

M. R.

1 Fr Accinelli has been here: at Piacenza; how angry he was because you

took the Sister. The Superior Francesca, needing a nursing Sister

for the hospital, had taken her from the Genoa house, so that Fr Accinelli, as

administrator of the house, had been put out. Try to smooth things over; Sr.

A. Francesca writes to M. Rosa on 1 December: “I long for the moment to see him

(Fr Accinelli) to tell him the reason”.

2 I am carrying a good load (dose) of suffering, with great trust in God,

while feeling the weakness of the flesh. “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak”

3 what cold we had to suffer, and what humiliation.

your affectionate Servant, Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

A.M.F.

My Anna,

1. I wish you happy holidays, with greetings for holy Christmas and a happy New Year.

2. I am sending you some things for my dear jewels, Rosa's family;1 they are all new and from a healthy person, they may be sure. For pity's sake, let them pray that I may obtain it; it concerns, as you well know, that person's readmission.2

Goodbye; pray, for pity's sake.

Most Reverend Eminence,

1. A holy duty obliges me to send you our little Rules, just printed with the permission of the Sacred Congregation, as a trial, so as to test whether they are suited to continuing our present way of working and our customs. II. INDEX OF THE RECIPIENTS OF THE LETTERS

1. ARATA (Lawyer) VINCENZO. In January 1873 Mother Rosa, having gone to Foligno to found a new house, called on the Prefect as well as the Bishop and the Mayor. The 1873 General Yearbook of Italy shows that Foligno had a Sub-Prefecture office dependent on the Prefecture of Perugia, headed at that time by the Sub-Prefect, the lawyer Vincenzo Arata. We also learn that he later served as Prefect in various cities: Novara, Modena, Messina, Pisa, etc. L 9.

2. ALTIERI (Princess of Viano) BICE. A woman of faith and of deep moral and religious sensitivity, she was actively engaged in charitable works for the poor when she met Mother Rosa in Rome, and she gladly supported her wish to employ her Daughters in the service of the city's poor. As President of the St Monica Catholic Circle, she entrusted to her a school for poor girls at Tor de' Specchi. She helped find the premises (L 38), set up the school and keep it running well, visiting and encouraging the Sisters (L 45), and later chose the Daughters of Saint Anne, in preference to other Congregations, for the School that the Holy Father Pius IX intended to open at the Parrocchietta (L 61, n. 6). To the Mother, who was not well acquainted with the “Roman world”, she was a valuable and enlightening adviser regarding the works and the people involved in them. The Mother also asked for her support in seeking approval of the Rules through the authoritative intervention of her husband, Prince Ludovico, with the Secretary of the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, Mgr Vitelleschi. Her friendship with Mother Rosa continued in mutual visits and correspondence. Her letters and notes, 33 in all (from 1873 to 1883), are preserved in the AFSA. L 38; 45; 53; 205.

3. BARNABÒ (Marchioness) COSTANZA, née DEL GALLO. The Mother first turned to her asking for a word of recommendation to her brother-in-law Cardinal Alessandro, Prefect of “Propaganda fide” (L 81). Several years later the Marchioness was nursed by the FSA during a serious illness and, grateful for their diligent care, gave the Institute the sum of £ 5,000, which was used to provide the Sisters with a dwelling

better suited to their work. In 1898 a new house was in fact bought in Via Denti. Cf. AFSA. L 81.

4. BIAGINI (Sr. A. Augusta) CATERINA, daughter of Biagio and Maria Prato. The Mother, having gone to Foligno in 1872, had met the Biagini family and had been helped by them in her first contacts with the local authorities. The young woman felt called to follow her; she entered the Institute on 22 March 1873, received the religious habit on the following 17 May and the name Sr. A. Augusta. After six months of formation in the Mother House she was sent to Sampierdarena as superior, in November of the same year 1873. The Mother entrusted her to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa, who, as superior of the hospital Community at Sampierdarena, visited her to advise and encourage her. In spite of this, she proved unsuited to the task entrusted to her and to religious life. Cf. Lett. 187, 1-2; 285, n. 3; etc. She left the Institute in November 1874 (cf. L 364, n. 1). She was first taken in by the Daughters of Charity in Turin (cf. L 383); later she returned to her family. Of Mother Rosa's letters to her only one survives, found among the papers of Sr. A. Francesca Camisa and published here as no. 271.

5. BIAGINI (Sr. A. Carlotta) ANNA, daughter of Biagio and Giovanna Cincolani. The Mother, returning to Rome from one of her usual visits to Foligno, took her along as a guest on 5 October 1873. The young woman stayed at Piacenza, in the Mother House, and at Genoa with Carlotta and Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino (L 110,1; 112,4; 120, n. 3). Later she asked to join the Daughters of Saint Anne, like her sister. She received the habit on 30 September 1873 and took the name Sr. A. Carlotta. Mother Rosa trusted her, sent her as superior to Pennabilli, to the newly founded community, then transferred her on 27 July 1874 to Ferrara (L 291), and finally appointed her superior of the Mother House. But Sr. A. Carlotta was not faithful to her and went so far (we cannot know from what senseless motive) as to conceive the wicked plan of killing the one who had chosen her to be at her side in a position of considerable responsibility in the most important house of the Institute. The Mother speaks of it at length in the Memorie, 4.3, pp. 39-47. Inwardly enlightened about what the Sister intended to do against her, she called her and revealed her wicked plan, and succeeded in touching her heart and making her aware of the gravity of the evil she was about to commit. The Sister ended by confessing her fault and found “in the boundless charity”

of the Mother “relief, remedy, comfort and healing” through sincere repentance. With these and other moving words, from Cortemaggiore, where on the Mother's advice she had made a course of Spiritual Exercises and a sincere general confession, she once more opened her heart to her in a letter full of repentance, devotion and resolutions for a new life, on 2 May 1875, before returning to her family (cf. AFSA, D3, Csls, 3). The letters to her published in this volume number 31.

6. BIANCHI (Father) RAIMONDO. Born in 1831 at Chiusanico (IM), died in Rome on 25 June 1885. He entered the Dominicans in 1847, at Perugia. In 1867 he was appointed Procurator General of the Order. He held important posts in the Roman Curia: Consultor of the Congregation of Propaganda Fide, of the Congregation of the Council and of the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars; Master of the Sacred Palace. In 1873 he was entrusted with the revision of the Constitutions of the Daughters of Saint Anne, and for this reason he had dealings with Mother Rosa aimed at clarifying, on both sides, particular aspects and points of the spirit of the Institute and of the Constitutions. Their relationship was marked by esteem, trust and mutual deference. L 114; 134; 160; 169.

7. BIANCHI (Fr) VINCENZO. He was parish priest of “S. Antonino Martire” at Polverigi (AN) when in 1874 he turned to Mother Rosa Gattorno asking for information about the Institute and its charitable activities. Arrangements were then begun for the FSA to go there, and the Foundress was inclined to send them, but owing to local circumstances no positive conclusion was reached, as the Parish Priest Rodolfo Ragnini told Mother Benedetta Carrega many years later, on 20 April 1907, when asking for the FSA to be sent to the nursery school to be opened at Polverigi. Cf. AFSA, Foundations. L 286; 293.

10. BORGHESE (Duchess) AGNESE. She was born in Rome on

5.5.1836. At the age of 18 she married Rodolfo Boncompagni Ludovi-

si, Prince of Piombino and Duke of Sora, by whom she had six children: Ugo, Luigi, Guendalina, Maddalena, Giuseppe and Maria. She was at Foligno in the “Villa Ludovisi” when Mother Rosa, called by the Grampini sisters in 1872, went there to open a new work. The Marchioness took to heart the Foligno foundation and later that of Oppello, and devoted herself to them with commitment and charity so that the girls might receive an excellent human and Christian formation in both schools. To M. Rosa she was more than a friend: she esteemed and admired her, helped her with advice and gifts of money, and maintained the Oppello school at her own expense. She introduced her to her good friends who were willing to help her. To the Sisters, by her authoritative and affectionate presence, she was a true mother who knew how to advise and bring out the best. Her correspondence with the Mother runs from 1873 to 1900. 90 letters to M. Rosa survive, 3 to M. Benedetta Carrega and two to the superior of Oppello. Cf. AFSA, Friends. L 16; 18; 96.

12. BRUSCHI (Sr. A. Eletta) GIULIETTA, born at Piacenza on 25.4.1852, received the FSA habit on 19.5.1872 at Sampierdarena. 17. CARREGA (Sr. A. Benedetta) ANNA. Daughter of Marquis Antonio Benedetto and Camilla D'Aste, she was born at Genoa on 28.5.1842. She lost her Mother at the age of [...] and was placed by her father, together with her sister Emilia, in a boarding school run by the French Ladies at Nice, to receive an education suited to her social position. At Genoa she met M. Rosa and was struck by her personality and her strong moral and spiritual influence. In January 1874 she told her of her decision to follow her (L 172) and went to Rome, where she received the habit of the Daughters of Saint Anne in the Chapel of the monastery of the Oblate Sisters of St Frances of Rome at Tor de' Specchi. In premises next to that monastery the Daughters of Saint Anne had opened a school for poor girls. In 1875, on the death of Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino, she became Mother Rosa's Secretary, and in 1900 she was unanimously elected to succeed her as Superior General. She died on 9.2.1915. L 268; 269; 317.

18. CARREGA (Marchioness) EMILIA, sister of Mother Benedetta, was born at Genoa on 12.11.1838, after four boys, and was followed in 1842 by Anna. She knew Rosa Gattorno and was her confidante and friend, as their correspondence shows, but did not feel called to follow her into religious life as her sister Anna did; she remained unmarried and devoted herself to good works. She died in Rome on 13.2.1919. She is buried at the Verano in the chapel of the Daughters of Saint Anne, at the wish of the Superior General of the time, Celsa Speranza. L 116; 181.

19. CAVALLETTI DURAZZO (Marchioness) MARIA. President of the “Pious Union of Lady Protectors of Young Women in Service” in Rome, founded in 1871, she wished to entrust to Mother Rosa the running of a boarding house in Trastevere for the care of young servant girls. She was on excellent terms with her and with the Sisters, directed some young women to the FSA, and worked to have M. Rosa extend her social and charitable work beyond Rome to Frascati and elsewhere. The Mother deservedly called her “our great

benefactress” (L 83). Nine of her letters to M. Rosa are preserved in the AFSA, whereas of those addressed to the Marchioness in 1873-74 only one survives, published here as no. 300.

20. COCCHELLA (Sr. A. Del S. Cuore) LUIGIA. Born at Genoa on 6.1.1848, she entered the Institute on 20.11.1868 and received the religious habit on 28.3.1869. In 1873 the Mother transferred her from Ferrara to Rome, appointing her Superior of the Trastevere house, but she proved unequal to the task. The Mother admonished her several times, as the correspondence shows. After some time, in January 1874 to be precise, she went home for lack of vocation. L 118; 125; 137; 157; 162; 167.

III. INDEX OF NOTABLE PERSONS NAMED IN THE CORRESPONDENCE

1. ACCINELLI (Priest) ANTONIO. Born in 1825. After ordination he exercised his priestly ministry at Genoa, largely in the metropolitan church of “S. Lorenzo”, of which he was custodian from 1873. A friend of the Gattorno family, he was very close to Mother Rosa, whom he considered worthy of honour and respect for her uncommon qualities and for the outstanding mission to which God was calling her. He believed in that mission and that call. He looked after the interests of Carlotta and Alessandro, left orphans; he was Mother Rosa's attorney for her father's estate. In the course of the “Ricchini case” (cf. Lettere 1, p. 529) he took the part of a strong and combative supporter in defending Mother Rosa's cause, kept her constantly informed of developments in the dispute and advised her on the steps to take. In her work as foundress he was a faithful and enthusiastic collaborator. “I see that God's blessing is upon the Daughters of Saint Anne, and so I shall do all I can to help them” (L of 18.4.1873 to M. Rosa). He did not belie this resolution. A good judge of people and things, he was as shrewd as he was valuable an administrator of the Genoa community; for many years (until 1880) he worked to make it fulfil as well as possible its twofold religious and social purpose. He gave it not only a good part of his time but himself, with great brotherly kindness, taking on heavy work when needed, such as moving (L of 23.11.1872 to M. Rosa) from one house to another, made necessary by the growing number of Sisters required to meet the ever more numerous requests from the sick. “I do it to help, in my littleness, the good these charitable daughters can do” (ibid.). The major expenses were naturally his responsibility, sometimes for other houses too; for the rest he advised what was best to do according to events and circumstances. He personally handled relations with the civil and religious authorities, especially the Curia; he accepted postulants, always with the Mother's approval; he saw to the smooth running of the home nursing service. He kept Mother Rosa informed of everything. He put before her difficulties, problems and situations as they arose (at Genoa, Sampierdarena and Sestri) and the needs of the Sisters, pointing out to her the need and urgency of direct intervention. He some-

times opposed transfers she had decided on, foreseeing their bad consequences for the community; but always supremely respectful, after explaining his point of view he left her full freedom of action, apologizing to her.
