IV. THE FOUNDATIONS (1873-1874)

Mother Rosa's letters are – as already noted – a historical source of primary importance for knowledge of the Institute's development and life as regards people, places and events. In number, span of time and richness of content they offer such abundant and detailed material as to allow a well-documented historical reconstruction in its various aspects. For the subject that concerns us here – the foundations (but also for many others) – it should be noted that, given the nature of the letters, written for the most part under the pressure of the moment and the need to give advice, practical suggestions and news, the material is not arranged chronologically by subject or area of interest. Each letter is a fragment of life captured at a particular place and moment, with freshness, lively feeling and wealth of detail. To connect, through Mother Rosa's letters read together with those of her correspondents, the fragments of that life in the dynamism of its unfolding, and to read them as a single continuous subject, is the aim of the notes on the foundations set out below.

A historical aim, then, intended also to help the reader grasp an organic overall view of the correspondence and to make easier the correct interpretation of single letters and groups of letters related in content and purpose. (Cf. Lettere 1, p. 35).

1. FOLIGNO. School and home nursing of the sick

It is the first in time of the houses opened in these two years. The proposal to take her Daughters to Foligno had been made to her some time before, and it had seemed to her a sign from heaven that a former postulant, Colomba Grampini, who had entered the Mother House in 1869 wishing to become a Daughter of Saint Anne and had left after little more than a month, should ask her, together with her sister Nemisia Maria, to found a house in their town, offering her their own dwelling. The plan, attractive as it was, proved anything but easy to carry out; a long wait was needed. Like the others, this work of God too had to ripen in prayer and sacrifice.

In February 1872 the Mother, on the occasion of a journey to Rome, decided to go to Foligno (cf. Lettere 2, L 174), but nothing could be settled. 1872 passed amid hopes and renewed invitations from the two benefactresses, who meanwhile tried to involve various ladies and other prominent people in their plan (cf. L 299, 304). A new favourable opportunity came for Mother Rosa in January 1873 with another journey to Rome. She arrived at Foligno with Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino on the 15th, firmly convinced that this time it would succeed. With her energy and innate organizing ability, although in very poor health – “I am so ill that God alone sees what I suffer... I have so much pain that every moment I felt I was going to faint...” (L 12) – she managed to push through that contested business, which required uncommon abilities and great commitment. She visited the religious and civil dignitaries of the place: Bishop, Prefect (L 9, 10), Mayor, priests, religious and various gentlemen more or less disposed to welcome the new religious, whose presence seemed superfluous, since two communities of Daughters of Charity were already working there, in the hospital and the orphanage. She had several meetings with the Duchess Agnese di Sora Piombino and obtained the promise of her moral support and a small subsidy (L 16; 18). She wrote to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa to send the four Sisters assigned to the new work (L 8 and 11), and as soon as they arrived she saw to their lodging in a dwelling kindly lent by a Lady in the hamlet of Carpello, a kilometre from the town, until the tenants vacated the Grampini house. She stayed with them two days, initiating them into a community life woven of prayer, work and devotion to the needs of poor people, in complete trust in providence. They would earn their bread by the work of their own hands (sewing, embroidery, etc.) and accept alms and small gifts in kind. “I am at Carpello, the house is pleasant, everything lovely and good” (L 12).

Returning to Foligno on the 23rd to sign the deed of gift of the house, she left again the same day at 1 p.m. for Rome (ibid.).

The Sisters – Sr. A. Carmelina Carretta (superior), Sr. A. Ermelinda Solenghi, Sr. A. Pierina Tea and Sr. A. Gerolama Piralli – lose no time in putting the Mother's advice and directions into practice. The superior writes to her almost every day with encouraging reports. On 27 January: “every day no fewer than nine girls and two boys come to learn to read and the catechism... they bring their work too”; very soon they begin home nursing; they ac-

cept sewing work and embroider; “the work goes on, we have so much to sew, and stockings, slippers, crochet (lace), and if we had four hands we would not be idle” (23.3.73).

There was no lack of work and no lack of bread. To a religious who expressed doubts about that kind of poor life, Sr. A. Carmelina replied: “The poorer we are, the more the Lord will see that we lack nothing” (ibid.). And every day providence came in the simplest and most unexpected forms: three loaves, five oranges, three fine big cabbages, etc., accompanied by the hearts and smiles of poor, humble people rich in goodness. Sr. A. Gerolama's illness created some difficulty, but the good people who were by now taking an interest in the poor FSA – the Duchess Agnese di Sora, Maria Grampini, the two Superiors of the Daughters of Charity – helped ease the difficulties and offered help and advice. The Mother followed them, writing personally or having Vincenza write. That life lasted little more than a month. Informed in good time that the house was now free (L 29), the Mother went to Foligno again (L 56, 51) to move the Sisters.

New hardships, new labours in the bare, empty house; there was nothing but a few iron bedsteads she had sent earlier. “We are completely without everything and are looking about. I hope that here too the good God will console us and send us what we need” (L 56). The Duchess of Sora sent something: “oil, wine, chairs and other necessary things; none of the other ladies of the town stirred” (V. RAPALLINO, Memorie fondazione di Foligno). Indifference from the “good”, hostility from the enemies of religion. These did not stop at verbal abuse and written threats; they passed to deeds, trying to burn down the house by setting fire to the door. The Mother mentions it in passing to Sr. A. Francesca on 13 March '73: “I can barely hold the pen, I am very unwell, first from the fright of last night, then I received 4 letters, all with a good dose of wormwood” (L 60). “Amid so many tribulations”, indeed strengthened by “suffering”, she organized the house and the work. She went to the Bishop again and obtained ample approval. He wished to visit the house and brought significant gifts: a Way of the Cross, pictures, books. On that occasion the most suitable place for the little chapel was chosen. Meanwhile the Mother had taken Colomba Grampini into the Ferrara house as a guest; she had no religious vocation but wished to live in peace and seclusion (L 47). Urged by the need to open in Rome the other houses

under negotiation, she left Foligno on 17 March 1873 (L 62). She had no worries about the Sisters: they had already had good training at Carpello and were ready to start their activities: school for the little boys, teaching of women's work for the girls, and home nursing of the sick. The school, opened with few pupils, officially began on 21 April 1873, after authorization had been obtained from the school authorities. Nursing of the sick began on 20 March.

She returned to Foligno in June '73 (Letters 109-112) and in May '74 (Letters 259-262); she followed the community's progress through correspondence, always ready to intervene to remedy problems, either in person or through her secretary Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino, who did in fact go there in December 1874 to define the Sisters' activities clearly. On this M. Rosa wrote to her: “I too agree with the Duchess (Agnese di Sora) about not taking resident girls, so they have enough when there are: a school for boys, one for girls and the looms I am sending you today...” (L 377). At the end of the visit Sr. A. Vincenza sent her “news of immense consolation”: ...“here the house is doing very well, both as regards the nuns and providence... the people of Foligno are generous... the girls and boys are increasing a great deal... as for the sick, we do not know how to satisfy them all”. (Cf. L 373; 377; 378; 379; 381; 383).

Cf. V. RAPALLINO, Memorie fondazione di Foligno: AFSA, B.3.78; Carretta Sr. A. Carmelina, Letters: AFSA, D2, Carpello; Foligno – Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino; ibid., F.25. Mgr Pietro Tosti: Summarium pp. 342-352. Virga Jesse, 1987, 3.

2. OVADA (AL). Hospital

Negotiations for sending the FSA to the Hospital of “S. Antonio” at Ovada had begun in October 1872 (cf. Lettere 2, L 317; 321), and the Mother, knowing she had to go to Rome, had chosen in good time the Sisters to be assigned to that work; while waiting for the order to send them, she wrote from Rome to the President, Marco Montano, repeating her offer to send, besides the three Sisters requested, a fourth whom she would maintain “at her own expense” (L 17; 22). Unable to accompany them, she appointed Fr Accinelli and Sr. A. Francesca Camisa as her representatives (L 37). They were received with great honour and praise on 17

February 1873 by the authorities and the people. Everyone was convinced that with the Sisters there the hospital would at last function... as a hospital. Inaugurated on 15 August 1867, despite the good intentions of the Administrators and the good will of the doctor, it had never been made to work decently. Sr. A. Francesca, at first sight, sketches the situation in a letter to the Mother: “You cannot imagine the filth... the waste of things is beyond belief... no regulations... there are so many abuses that it really does not look like a hospital, it looks like a tavern; people come and go without asking anyone” (L of 19.2.1873). Without losing time or complaining, she sets to work. First of all cleaning utensils, walls and floor; putting the linen room in order and making an inventory; arranging the kitchen (even cutlery for the patients is lacking), etc. With her in facing the “heavy toil” are Sr. A. Giacomina Schenardi, Sr. A. Tommasina Viterbo, Sr. A. Virginia Gaggi and Sr. A. Geronima Piralli. They are entrusted with general coordination of services, nursing, the linen room and the kitchen (L 40). Kept minutely informed and consulted, Mother Rosa advises Francesca on what seems best to reconcile community life with hospital service. She suggests guidelines for the superior to follow; she encourages: “Everything you have done, you have done well” (L 40); she admonishes: “I am displeased with you because you wear yourself out too much, and the others too. Some of the heavy work you can have done by a daily woman” (L 56). She insists that Francesca obtain an increase in the number of Sisters: “If home nursing is added, if possible, at least 6 religious” (L 49).

Sr. A. Francesca, having got the community well started, arranged its spiritual care and organized the hospital service, assigning each Sister her task, returned to Piacenza on 10 March. For further practical difficulties the Superior and Sisters would turn to her, but above all the Mother took responsibility for directing the house. As with the other houses, the superior continued to send her frequent reports, receiving encouragement and direction. The Sisters earned the esteem and affection of the hospital staff, the patients and the townspeople. Particularly kind to them was Fr Tito Borgatta. He, who had been the first to approach Mother Rosa to ask for the Sisters, considered it his duty to follow and help them over the years. He was a good father to them and a watchful adviser to Mother Rosa, keeping up a correspondence with her to promote the good of the Sisters and of the work.

3. ROME. Tor de' Specchi. Elementary School

Mother Rosa, having to go to Rome fairly often to deal with the approval of the Rules and other matters of the Institute, wished to own a house, however small, which would serve the twofold purpose of planting in the “holy city” the little seed of God's work, a long-cherished wish, and of providing a base that would free her from having to lodge in private houses, as she had often done. She had therefore asked her friends Rosa Parodi and Anna Clotilde Grasso for their prayers (cf. Lettere 2, L 56) and trusted in the efficacy of those prayers with the Lord. But she knew how to tune in to God's will and wait for His good pleasure. Almost two years passed before her Rosa's “prediction” came true. She was helped to fulfil her keen wish by Princess Bice Altieri (cf. Index II, 2). Having decided to entrust a school for poor girls to the Daughters of Saint Anne, the Princess was able to offer premises (L 37), placed at the disposal of the Catholic Circle she chaired by the superior of the Monastery of the Oblates of St Frances of Rome, Marchioness Maddalena Galleffi (L 38). The Mother was overjoyed. Going promptly to see them, she thanked the distinguished benefactress: “I found everything lovely, even too much for us...”. But the premises needed adapting to make them suitable for the community and the school. While the workmen prepared the rooms, carrying out the design of the monastery's architect, the Mother, with Sr. A. Vincenza's help, set about arranging what the foundation needed. Everything was lacking, but providence came with small signs to nourish their faith: a piece of furniture (L 45); the first enrolments of poor girls brought by their mothers (L 52). She wrote to the Mother House to send sheets, pillowcases and other linen, and straw mattresses (which Fr Agostino would have filled with straw), and also gave suitable instructions for the Sisters who, when she called, were to leave for Rome (L 46; 54; 55). Obliged on 4 March to go to Foligno to organize that work (L 55), she was replaced by Sr. A. Vincenza, who, with Carlotta, was lodging, like the Mother, “at the house of the good widow Signora Celestina Pisoni, in Via delle Colonne dei Massimi” (L 18). She returned to Rome on 17 March (L 64); by the 24th the house was ready, the workmen having finished (cf. Rapal-

lino to Camisa: 22.3.73); but “everything was lacking; we were still without beds; for some time I slept with Rapallino on the floor in a corner of the room that served as refectory, on a little straw, with the back of a chair as pillow; the Mother had a small straw mattress full of insects, given her by the soldiers through Fr Agostino Donadio”; so wrote Sr. A. Crocifissa Fiocchi, one of the first Sisters, who had come with the Mother from Foligno to serve as cook. Princess Altieri, to make the Sisters' rest less uncomfortable, lent two mattresses taken from her daughters' beds and two pillows, and sent a coffee pot, 4 cups, coffee and sugar (AFSA, Friends). In that atmosphere of joyful poverty the school for poor girls was born; the teaching was entrusted to Sr. A. Eletta Bruschi, who was also the first superior, and to Sr. A. Eufrosina Pizzoni. Three other Sisters helped in the house and, when needed, nursed the sick at home. They could meet only a few requests because there were so few of them (as the Rule prescribed, they had always to go to the sick in pairs, by day and by night), nor could their number be increased, limited as they were by the cramped premises. The Mother usually resided at Tor de' Specchi, moving to the other three communities as organization and the Sisters' needs required. Carlotta was with her, while Sr. A. Vincenza was at the “House in Trastevere” (L 109; 111; 113).

The school, set up through the interest of the Ladies of the “St Monica Catholic Circle” and placed under their patronage, began immediately after Easter (which that year fell on 15 April) (L 52) and ran normally with more or less regular attendance. The government syllabus was followed; catechism was taught, and sewing and embroidery as well. At the examinations, as a test of learning and diligence, pupils and teachers displayed their skill and effort to the Princess-President and the ladies of the Circle. By way of encouragement and approval they received kind congratulations and some small useful prize. The “Circle” had limited financial means. Apart from the extraordinary expenses of setting up the school, its normal contribution was generally limited to school materials. The Sisters were maintained by the Institute. Mother Rosa had told the Ladies clearly that she wanted nothing for the Sisters; she herself would maintain them. On 8 November '73 the superior reported: “We spend only on what is necessary. I have £ 51 in all, but it will not be enough for next month.

Here all begging is forbidden. It is hard for me to tell you that I am poor”. But providence came, now with small gifts of money, now with presents that were always useful and welcome: candles and some furnishings for the chapel. Particularly fond of them, and a neighbour not only in location, the Superior of the Monastery of the Oblates (L 38, n. 1) almost every day sent some small present from the nuns' kitchen, usually a “dish she thought the dear Sisters would enjoy, not so much for the quantity” as for the kindness that came with it. To the 40 schoolgirls who on 22 July brought her name-day greetings with a little recitation, she gave a made-to-measure dress (L Sup. Bruschi to M. Rosa). Mother Rosa left Rome after five months of almost continuous residence (on 30 June 1873, L 109), having settled the four houses (L 99; 104; etc.). She returned in January 1874 and again took up residence at Tor de' Specchi (L 175). The problem of the Rules had not been resolved. Father Bianchi had almost completed drafting the Constitutions, and it was essential for her to examine them to make sure they matched the spirit of the Institute and to make any necessary observations and corrections before the text was handed to the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars.

She also thought it necessary to remain in Rome to follow the progress of the case and hasten its conclusion. There was also need to visit the communities and see whether everything was proceeding according to the directions she had given.

At Tor de' Specchi a dispute had arisen, caused by the distrust of certain ladies and fed by unfounded rumours and suspicions against Mother Rosa. Since she had a plate of hot soup distributed daily to the pupils, the Ladies of the Circle had expressed their displeasure, convinced that she would charge the expense to the Circle's accounts. They complained of a financial irregularity, accusing her of having collected from the Parish Priests assisted by the Circle a certain contribution that they were supposed to pay. She clarified the situation in a letter to the President (L 205), and the sincere harmony with her collaborators that she loved and fostered as a sign of the sincere, active charity that was to animate all in the one ideal of charity was restored.

The work of the Daughters of Saint Anne in Rome was blessed with the gift of many vocations. “Here I am accepting postulants as fast as I can”, she told Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino (L 234), who at Piacenza was preparing the premises for a very spacious pos-

tulancy. Meanwhile, in the Tor de' Specchi house, the postulant Anna Carrega was preparing, under the Foundress's guidance (Lett. 220; 228; 231; 246; 247), to join the Daughters of Saint Anne. She received the religious habit on 19 April 1874 in the chapel of the Oblates' monastery. “Anna is ours, she is called Sr. A. Benedetta” (L 249).

She would succeed Mother Rosa in governing the Family of Saint Anne. Cf. Letters of Bice Altieri, AFSA, Friends; Letters of Sr. A. Eletta di Gesù Bruschi, ibid., F 35. 1873-74. Letters of Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino, ibid., F25. 1873-74.

4. ROME. Parrocchietta – Elementary School

Speaking of accepting the school in Via delle Fornaci, Mother Rosa had specified to Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino: “For that country house too I shall send linen, whatever she wants” (L 61). She is referring to the school the Holy Father wanted to open at the place called the “Parrocchietta”, where the Holy See owned a large vineyard with a house attached. She had gone there with Mgr Augusto Negrotto and at first sight, accustomed as she was not to be fussy when charity and the good of “poor and needy humanity” were at stake, she had been very pleased: “On Saturday (5 April 1873) we shall go and occupy the Pope's (house), a lovely one for air and convenience, outside the Porta S. Pancrazio, excellent air; a school there too”; so she wrote to Countess Isabella Caracciolo (L 72). She also mentioned it to Mgr Salvatore Vitelleschi on 5 April: “When I return from Mgr Negrotto's country place, where I am going to open a school, I shall call on Your Excellency” (L 76). Government authorization having been obtained (L 78), the school began with a good initial number of over 30 pupils, very happy, as were their mothers, and eager to learn. The house was by no means in good condition: a dangerous staircase, windows without shutters and some without glass, small rooms. Princess Altieri, on a friendly visit, was unfavourably struck by the Sisters' airless and dark refectory. Mgr Negrotto saw to ordering desks for the school, some furniture, a large “cupboard” for the girls' books, coat stands and other furniture, a picture of Saint Anne and various furnishings for the little chapel, and every time he went he brought some little present for the pupils. Much appreciated was the cloth to make an apron for each of them. The teachers: Sr. A. Camil-

la Bonetti for the older girls and Sr. A. Ambrogia Civardi for the little ones, helped by the Superior Sr. A. Domenica Marchesini, taught school subjects and catechism in the morning; in the afternoon they helped the other Sisters with practical lessons in women's work. The school stayed open in the summer months too, because the girls were free from farm work, whereas they stayed home to help with the grape harvest in October. The pupils did well in their examinations. “Mother – the superior wrote on 12 September – I cannot tell you how well these girls did; they were examined in catechism, history, arithmetic, reading, writing and Italian before Mgr Negrotto and other dignitaries he brought with him... the poor girls are jumping for joy... everyone said they never expected such an examination at the Parrocchietta”. Towards mid-October, the older girls having also returned to school, 96 girls were regularly enrolled, and the school ran at its usual pace until 4 p.m.; no later, the mothers asked, because “these poor creatures have long stretches of road” and it is dangerous to be on the roads after dark. There was a good understanding with the families. “The ‘vineyard folk’ are so fond of us; they bring fruit, wine, eggs, flour, an occasional chicken”: very useful gifts which, added to the 50 lire a month punctually handed to the Superior by Mgr Negrotto, almost always allowed the books to balance at the end of the month, except in winter because of heating costs, indispensable in the icy house. In the summer months the Mother had thought it good to send the Sisters of Tor de' Specchi to the Parrocchietta in turns, two at a time, for about ten days, to rest and enjoy the good country air (L 310). Mother Rosa was pleased with the success of the school and community, which she regarded as the Holy Father's gift, blessed by him with particular kindness. She thanked him in words of touching gratitude: “The thought Your Holiness had of entrusting to us two schools (she meant also the one in Via delle Fornaci), maintained by your hand, fills me with joy and leaves me speechless... Holiness, I would like to say too much to you! May my God be my interpreter by granting you the graces you desire...” (L 98).

The Pope gladly received the Daughters of Saint Anne of the Roman houses in private audience together with the pupils and their families, and took an interest in their work. Encouraged, the Superiors never failed to ask him for “a special blessing” for the Mother, about whom he would then ask for news.

The school went well, to general satisfaction. “My Mother, oh, how much work we have; our house is always full of girls and new ones keep coming” (Sup. Domenica, L to M. Rosa, 20.10.73). All idyllic, then, in the little country school among the vineyards?

The house, in the parts reserved for the Sisters under the roof, was a disaster. The Pope too had been informed, and at the audience of 19 October '73 he had said: “I hear it rains a great deal in the house, poor nuns, but have no fear, I shall see to sending the masons as soon as possible” (L 20.10.73). The masons came more than once, but thorough repairs were needed, not patching. “Although the masons have been, it still rains in two places: here in the dormitory, and as for the chimney, the more they work on it the more it rains” (L 8.11.73); ...“when it rains we cannot even cook dinner, so much water comes through the roof over the kitchen” (L 17.11.73).

To the winter hardships were added others: cramped quarters, quite inadequate for the ever-growing number of pupils; discomfort: the Sisters' dormitory was a loft under the roof, so low that one had to stoop to enter; the distance from Rome, which made communication difficult. They had to rely on the carter Giovanni Casadio, who offered to carry the post, collecting it from the other houses, or to take a Sister in his “cart”. The Mother “founded her houses from little”, Rapallino had told Princess Bice Altieri (Rap. to M. Rosa: 12.3.73). The “poor FSA” could have no other style than that of poverty and obscurity.

Cf. Letters of Sr. A. Domenica Marchesini, AFSA, D2; D3. Letters of Sr. A. Eletta di Gesù Bruschi, ibid., F35. 1873-74.

5. ROME. Via delle Fornaci – Elementary School

On 12 March 1873 Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino reported to Mother Rosa the proposal of Princess Bice Altieri di Viano: having been given a free hand, she wanted to entrust them with the school the Holy Father intended to open outside the city. “She told me there is a lovely little chapel already finished and that the Pope, that is, Mgr Pacca, would pay about 50 fr. a month”. “The ladies of the Catholic Circle would see to setting up the school and the house, except for the linen. But she told me the air is not very good”. The

Mother, as usual, replied by return of post: “You can answer her that to serve the Pope I would make any sacrifice, even of my very life, and that she may count on all the religious Daughters of Saint Anne and dispose of them as she pleases in every way” (L 61).

The premises, a small villa belonging to Mgr Bartolomeo Pacca, Palatine Prelate, stood on the outskirts of the city, not far from the Vatican, in an unhealthy area not only because of the “not very good air”, as the good Princess of Viano had hastened to report, but above all because of the deplorable cultural and economic underdevelopment of the people – reasons that made the work urgent and indispensable. The first Superior was Sr. A. Eugenia Gaudenzi; the teaching was entrusted first to Sr. A. Panasia Bellardi (L 49) and later to Sr. A. Irene Carmeli (L 343; 348). The Sisters also helped in the parish, run by Fr Giulio del S. Cuore di Maria of the Discalced Trinitarians, guiding and forming the Children of Mary. “Yesterday – the Mother wrote to Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino – I attended a magnificent ceremony at the Fornaci; they established the Congregation of the Children of Mary; Mgr Negrotto conferred the medals; procession, all dressed in white, a sermon. Soon they will establish it at the Parrocchietta too” (L 234). These good results of the Sisters' apostolate repaid her for the many troubles this work had caused her. The Sisters had all fallen ill, so much so that they had moved to the Trastevere house to be treated for malarial fever and had temporarily closed the school. One of them, Sr. A. Michelina Morelli, did not recover and died some time later. In October the school reopened normally, and the year ended with “a display of studies and an exhibition of work”. This news was reported with satisfaction to the Mother by the new President of the St Monica Circle, Maria Schneider, successor to Princess Bice Altieri di Viano.

Cf. Letters of Sr. A. Eugenia Gaudenzi, AFSA, D 2. Sr. A. Eletta Bruschi, ibid., F35. 1873-74.

6. ROME – Trastevere. Home for domestic servants

The start of this work was announced by Mother Rosa to Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino on 9 April: “On Wednesday we shall enter the Cavalletti House” (L 80). This laconic phrase contains two historically important pieces of information: the opening date, which, ac-

cording to the universal calendar, corresponds to 16 April, and the other, no less interesting: the purpose of the work. The Marchioness Maria Cavalletti Durazzo was in fact President of the “Primary Pious Union of Lady Protectors of Young Women in Service”, founded in 1871, and the work was directed and sponsored by her. Mother Rosa had readily agreed to accept this institution, which corresponded well to the Institute's charitable aims in favour of girls at risk. Many of them, poor and needing to earn something for themselves and their families, sought work and found nothing better than to become “servants”. About ten of them were lodged in the Trastevere house entrusted to the FSA. Taught the first rudiments of learning and Christian doctrine and trained in household work – cleaning, washing and ironing and, for those who wished, sewing and embroidery – they were then placed with morally reliable families. In the correspondence of this period the Sisters usually called the work the “Trastevere House”. The Mother incidentally gives its address: Piazza S. Agata, 1 (L 306).

The Pious Union did not have enough funds to run the work properly. It had been agreed that it would give a daily subsidy of one lira for each of the eight girls. For the four Sisters in charge, no payment. The Mother, there being enough room, had also placed six Sisters there for free home nursing, which was much in demand. To provide for their needs the Sisters had to find ways of earning at least their daily bread. They managed to find some sewing and ironing. Above all they took in families' dirty washing, washed, mended and ironed it. They had only a small terrace on which to hang it out. How much toil in winter, especially when it rained, taking it in still wet and hanging it out again! Yet they did not complain! The hours free from nursing the sick and from their educational tasks with the girls were filled with this heavy extra work.

Given the complexity and nature of the work, Mother Rosa took care to choose “very reserved, serious, capable and obedient Sisters of a certain bearing” (L 99). First Superior: Sr. A. Del Sacro Cuore Cocchella, a Genoese who had seemed suitable to her but who still needed to mature. She started her on her difficult task, leaving Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino beside her to guide her,

who knew the situation of the house and the people well (L 85 and 86), having been there to get the foundation properly started while awaiting the Superior's arrival. She then followed her by writing to her in her own hand, helping her to solve the various problems as they arose (Lett. 118; 125; 137; 157; 162; 167). She had drawn up a set of regulations for the house, specifying the aims of the work and the role of each person. Everyone had to keep to them, including the ladies of the “Pious Union”. Meanwhile the sick were increasing and were pleased with the work of the Sisters, who gladly sacrificed themselves day and night to relieve the sufferings of so many poor people. But the “Ladies” complained of their presence in the house and accused them of living at the expense of their institution. Another problem was the Superior, who did not prove equal to her task. The Mother was forced to replace her (L 199); Sr. A. Vincenza went to settle the situation and instruct the new Superior, Sr. A. Sofia Pasti (L 195; 196). Once good order had been restored, the Mother considered how to enlarge the work and made arrangements with Mgr Rinaldo Degiovanni, the administrator of the house, to buy a larger building. The Marchioness Maria Cavalletti, whom she consulted, left her free to act and at the same time said she was so pleased with the Sisters' work that she wanted them at Frascati too (L 300). There are no further references to the new premises in the correspondence of the period under review.

Cf. Letters of Sr. A. del S. Cuore Cocchella, AFSA, D2 – Letters of the Marchioness Maria Cavalletti Durazzo, AFSA, Friends.

7. PIACENZA. “Casa Poss”

Around 1870 the brothers Alessandro and Emilio Poss, Milanese of German origin, had opened at Piacenza, in Strada dell'Abbondanza, a silk-throwing mill employing 30 women aged 9 to 40 and 10 men aged 20 to 50, considered the largest in the province. The establishment had modern equipment for that time and could meet the needs of several cloth manufacturers. Emilio Poss asked Mother Rosa to let a number of her girls work in the mill, and she agreed, but not before making enquiries and setting out in a proper contract the conditions and terms of employment of the girls, for whom she was responsible. The corre-

spondence of the last months of 1873 and the whole of 1874 gives much information on the opening and development of the work. On 17 September 1873 Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino wrote from Ovada to the superior of the Mother House, Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: “The Mother tells me that the contract we made with Poss will come in a letter”. From other evidence it can be inferred that the girls, under the guidance and responsibility of Sr. A. Del Buon Pastore Dosi, had begun work in the mill in October, because Sr. A. Francesca told Mother Rosa on 8 November 1873: “At last Poss has paid Buon Pastore; she received 150 francs in all”. Mother Rosa, writing to Sr. A. Francesca, urges that Sr. A. Del Buon Pastore behave well (L 151) and specifies the number of girls: “There should be 40, I think that is what we said” (L 153).

It had also been agreed with Poss that he would house the workers and the supervising Sisters, providing suitable and equipped premises: dormitories, refectory, kitchen and a large chapel. The Mother would contribute the linen and furnishings for the chapel: “For Poss I have found everything; I am sending it all to Piacenza: chalice, pyx, chasubles...” (L 187). And for the chapel she asked the Holy Father for a special blessing, describing to him also how the work was organized: “The premises were built and fitted out as a factory, where there are already 18 religious directing and looking after more than 200 poor resident girls and 300 outside workers helping in that great silk works. The said gentleman, although a Protestant, has already given a very large room to make an internal oratory, which will hold more than 500 people” (L 213). She wanted the inauguration of the chapel, which took place on 12 April 1874, to be solemn and “without stinting... I would like there to be many priests... see that it is well decorated...” (L 242).

She protected and defended the girls' interests and rights. She would not let them go to live there until the rooms were dry and declared “fit for habitation” by the doctor (L 197). She protested strongly to Signor Emilio Poss, who “had got into the habit of punishing the girls by adding a slap or two” (L 277). Correcting, supervising and educating were the Sisters' task alone. She firmly supported the supervising Sisters' requests for improved hygiene in the premises (L 280) and asked for higher wages (L 365). To make Casa Poss (as it was usually called) work well, Sr. A. Francesca Camisa having left for Sampierdarena, she sent Sr. A. Vincenza there and kept in close touch by letter to enlighten and guide her in the individual

cases that arose (L 216; 234; etc.). “See that at Poss the girls are well looked after, and add some more nuns”, she wrote to her on 23 March '74 (L 232). The number of resident girls entrusted to the Sisters had grown because the Mother had extended the opportunity to work to others: to girls from the other houses of the Daughters of Saint Anne and to others recommended by parish priests. The factory therefore had girls from various places: Nizza Monferrato, Cremona, Genoa, Sampierdarena, Bramaiano, Soresina (L 219; 222; 224; 246; 254). Her chief aim in taking in the girls was their human advancement: to prepare them for life through a serious Christian, cultural and vocational formation suited to their state. She had them taught Christian doctrine; every Sunday they all attended Mass and catechism together in the large chapel (L Rapallino to M. Rosa: 21.4.74). She had set up evening classes entrusted to the teacher Onorata Colli. These ended each year with formal examinations attesting the progress made.

This work did not escape criticism. Mother Rosa took note of it but found nothing in conscience to reproach herself with. “Whatever Signor Poss does will be as it will be; meanwhile we give (the girls) food, we draw them out of sin, we teach them to love God! The Eternal Father will see to the rest” (L 234).

8. PENNABILLI (PS) – Elementary School – Nursery School – Home nursing

The President of the Congregation of Charity of Pennabilli, Signor Luigi Piccini, wrote to M. Rosa on 29 August 1873 asking her to open a house of her Institute there in order to “educate the girls and nurse the sick at home” until a hospital could be set up. The request was formally supported by the mayor Sebastiano Caliendi and desired by the Bishop, Mgr Luigi Mariotti. Mother Rosa replied in the affirmative to the first two (L 127; 128); she asked the Bishop for his pastoral blessing and received, with fatherly encouragement, the consoling promise: “I shall spare no effort to help you at all times” (AFSA, F 59,2). And since the Sisters were needed before the start of the school year (15 October), it was agreed to hasten their departure. Sr. A. Francesca Camisa would accompany Sr. A. Carlotta Biagini (superior), Sr. A. Adelaide Cervini and Sr. A. Dorotea Benedetti

(teachers) and Sr. A. Alessandrina Lodola (for general duties) to help them start the community well; with them Fr Accinelli, as the Mother's attorney, would sign the contract.

The dwelling was already prepared – the President had specified – “good and comfortable for the Sisters, furnished with everything necessary, with an internal school and an adjoining church likewise connected internally”. Told that from Rimini they would have to make the rest of the journey by carriage, taking five hours, they arranged to reach Rimini by train in good time. By six in the morning of 9 October they were there. They entered a church, and everyone took it as a good sign to find there a venerated image of Saint Anne, at whose altar Fr Accinelli celebrated Holy Mass. Leaving again at 7.30, they reached their destination at two in the afternoon, awaited and warmly received by the President and others. In the house the table was laid and dinner ready. The next day the agreement was signed, which stated among other things that the four Sisters “were to run the girls' schools in the 1st, 2nd and 3rd classes and the infant school, and that care of the sick was to be given as far as compatible with the schools and with the number of religious”. Sr. A. Francesca and, for his part, Fr Accinelli informed the Mother of everything, including the visit to the Bishop, whose see was at Pennabilli, and his cordial welcome (cf. AFSA, F24; AA1M, 94).

After the two escorts had left, the Sisters set to work. 35 pupils were enrolled in the Elementary School and as many in the Nursery School. There would be no lack of work. But all felt the burden of distance from the Mother in that village “on the top of a mountain so high that one really does not know how they managed to plant it there”; such was the first general impression, expressed jokingly by Sr. A. Francesca. The Mother followed Sr. A. Carlotta very closely, encouraging her and the Sisters: “Courage! The good God loves sacrifices...! Ah, yes, for His work one must go without sparing oneself...!”, and answering the superior's questions promptly with suitable advice. In every letter she insists on a few fixed points: observance of the Rules, prayer, care of health. “Let the food – she repeated – be wholesome and good”. School work was not compatible with home nursing. Once the school had opened she gave orders that they were not to go: “I do not want those who teach to go out nursing. If they want nurses, they will send for others” (L 135). This point – getting

the Congregation of Charity to accept two more Sisters, whom she would maintain at her own expense – recurs frequently in her correspondence with the superior (L 166; 175; 191; 193; 200; 217; 245). Her wish was finally granted: two Sisters would be regularly engaged for home nursing “at an annual salary of £ 75 each”.

9. SESTRI PONENTE.

Home nursing – School

Information on the founding and development of this work comes from the letters to Mother Rosa of Fr Antonio Accinelli, whom she had charged with negotiating the matter and then helping the work to run well. He kept her diligently informed. On 24 September 1873 he wrote to her: “I can tell you nothing definite about Sestri. On Sunday I spoke with one of the ‘Commission’ and said the nuns were ready to go as soon as they had prepared everything needed for lodging and maintenance”. On 25 October: “At Sestri they are doing all they can to call your Daughters soon; the house is almost ready; the alms-collectors (the FSA Sisters who had gone there begging) saw it and were pleased; it will not be long before they call us”. Mother Rosa, then at Genoa, held herself ready (L 149), and on 25 November she was able to tell Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: “Tomorrow I am going to Sestri; at last that house is opening; I shall need two more religious” (L 158). The house was therefore opened on 26 November 1873. The community of four Sisters, with Sr. A. Filomena Pugnaloni as superior, was to devote itself to home nursing. But from the very first days an obstacle blocked the work: the house was too far from Sestri and outside the municipality, so the Sisters received no calls to nurse the sick. Matters stood thus when on 10 December Fr Accinelli, having fully grasped the situation, tried to remedy it, promising her that he would do his best to have them moved into the town as soon as possible. By January the Sisters were already in the new house. Fr Accinelli himself gave her the good news on 10 January 1874: “Today I was at Sestri and found the nuns in perfect harmony; they are in the new house (Via Marina, 303, 3rd floor), they have some patients and things are going regular-

ly. Meanwhile I have arranged about the school, as follows. There is a pious bequest of £ 200 for teaching 15 poor boys catechism and the first lower class, plus £ 47 for books and paper... I have spoken about it to the Parish Priest and the Mayor, who administer it; now you see it would be a good opportunity to start... When the nun teacher comes, (the Sisters) will be six, and then they can do two shifts for the sick, whereas now they can take only one”. Hearing this, Mother Rosa hastened to act on the advice. She wrote to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: “See about the teacher for Sampierdarena and also for Sestri... He (Fr Accinelli) writes that they want us there too and are already ordering things for the school” (L 182). By 21 February the teacher was ready, and she asks that everything needed be prepared for her in the house (L 198). Sr. A. Francesca, however, judged the teacher's presence more necessary and appropriate at Sampierdarena, where the need was greater because of the resident girls (L 202). The Mother approved, as in other cases. She trusted her, because being on the spot she knew situations better and was well able to find the most immediate and suitable solution to every difficulty. She therefore charged her with going to the Sestri house as often as she could, now to advise the Superior, who did not feel equal to the task and asked to be relieved (L 274; 294), now about accepting a postulant: “I would like you to go to Sestri for a while to see, for that superior speaks to me of postulants. Meanwhile find out and write and tell me how that house is going” (L 207). The community is well established; it includes Sr. A. Del Salvatore Orsi, for home nursing, who also goes begging and in the afternoon manages to teach school and catechism to the boys. The Mother insists that she not be transferred (L 218; 287). Financially too there is some security, since through Fr Accinelli's efforts a Committee of benefactors has been formed, each of whom has undertaken to give a monthly donation (L Accinelli to M. Rosa: 10.1.1874). With the arrival of the teacher Sr. A. Enrichetta Salvatelli the school is organized. The people love and esteem the Sisters for their witness of active charity, and the Sisters try to meet everyone's expectations, spending themselves with sacrifice and humility as the Mother teaches them. A second timely move to larger and more suitable premises (L 270), and the arrival of the new superior, Sr. A. Giacomina Schenardi, whom Superior Francesca presents to the community and instructs

in the Mother's name (L 205), are the events that give the work dynamism and growth in the impetus of a faith that becomes active in charity and offers concrete answers, one after another, to the needs of those in want.

10. CORTEMAGGIORE. Hospital

On 17 September 1873 Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino, visiting Ovada with Mother Rosa, wrote to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa at Piacenza: “Next Saturday (20 September) they will bring a paper, the contract for the Cortemaggiore hospital, because that is what the Mother agreed with the doctor. Keep it locked away, and it will be signed when the Mother comes”. Archive documents show that some members of the “Administrative Commission of the Civil Hospices and Charitable Institutions” of Cortemaggiore, on the Mayor's instructions of 7 September 1873, had gone to Piacenza to confer with Mother Rosa and invite her to assign four Sisters of her Institute to the hospital service of that town. At the meeting a draft contract had been drawn up and their start had been provisionally fixed for the following 1 November. That date, however, was postponed by the hospital administrators for reasons unknown. The Mother expressed her puzzlement to Sr. A. Francesca: “I cannot understand about Cortemaggiore” (L 151). Some time later (on 9 December) she announced to Sr. A. Carlotta Biagini: “Tomorrow I am going to Cortemaggiore”. The opening date is therefore certainly 10 December 1873. She accompanied the Superior, Sr. A. Tommasina Viterbo, and with her arranged the allocation of duties to Sr. A. Elvira Persiani, Battistina Bertuzzi and Sr. A. Sofia Pasti. After four days she had to leave them; they were able to manage by themselves, and well. Certainly her presence gave confidence, but she wanted the Daughters of Saint Anne to be mature and responsible. “Your departure caused me very great sorrow – the Superior wrote to her – because there are a great many things to do, all the more in these first days here, so we have not yet got into practice... but although I find myself at a loss in many things, I still hope with the Lord's help to do little by little everything needed for the good order of the hospital” (L 13.12.73). A few days later, the chapel having to be fitted out, she sent Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino, who gave her a detailed re-

port: “The chapel is finished, so pretty... there is a fine Saint Anne; the Archpriest (Fr Domenico Costa) is all enthusiasm; he also brought a lovely lamp; in short he arranged it very nicely, and tomorrow morning he will come to say Mass, reserve the Blessed Sacrament and he also wants to give a fine talk. So now these Sisters have everything; it is a pleasure; nobody comes in now except at visiting time. Giovanni (the attendant) is very pleased and we keep him working; it seems impossible that there is always something to clean; he himself is amazed at so much dirt; in the sideboard and the pantry great quantities of playing cards are being found”. The Mother replies by return of post; she is sure that work will go very well (L 164). The Superior likes to draw confidence by leaning on the Mother's strength, wants to feel her near and tell her about herself, the Sisters and their hospital life: “Dear Mother, the further I go, the more I find that this office involves sacrifices, but I regard it as a cross and offer it to the Lord... we are all in good health, the hospital is always going well and there are many patients... These days we have had a lovely consolation, because a police sergeant who was here in the hospital and had not been to confession for 18 years has now confessed and received communion in our oratory” (L 11.2.74). The same day the Archpriest wrote to the Mother: “The town is extremely satisfied, and so is the ‘Commission’, the doctors too, and all the patients. The Sisters are cheerful, content, tireless and healthy. I have placed the Sacred Heart in their chapel; it has pride of place there, as is right”.

Serenity, harmony among the Sisters, devotion to the sick and fidelity to the Rule are the dominant notes in the correspondence of the energetic and intelligent Superior, determined to obey the Mother's directions and advice with docility: “I shall always send you these reports so that you may know how I conduct myself and therefore give me whatever warnings you think fit” (L 17.4.74). The Mother answers her directly or through Sr. A. Vincenza (L 220). Hearing that “they are cheerful and content though weighed down with fatigue” (L 29.3.74), she is moved and distressed and suggests that Sr. A. Vincenza send two more Sisters to help them. Another time she notes with some displeasure that the Superior spends too much (L 228). The Superior replies that she “is learning to economize well” (L 1.4.74). But this generous help cost her dear. The hospital bursar pointed out the irregularity to the Superior (the contract provided for only 4 Sisters) and also warned her of the rumours circulating

in the town: “If the Sisters come here, they say they come to eat the hospital's food or that I keep them on the hospital's goods”, the Superior writes (L 15.9.74). The Mother's intervention is prompt and decisive; she writes to Sr. A. Vincenza to warn the two Superiors (L 327), and to the President of the hospital. They are four again: “Sr. A. Cunegonda and Cristina have left, and their departure upset me a little... now everything gets done, but cleanliness cannot be kept up as before, and although there are only ten patients there is work all day long... it seems to me that four will not be able to go on doing everything well (note that the hospital had only one attendant)... we work all day without ever stopping, because we are always on our feet and going up and down” (L 2.10.74). The Mother then asks the “Commission” for permission to send at least one more Sister, whom she will maintain at her own expense. The Sisters, however, are serene: “Here in the hospital, dear Mother, we have a great deal of work, but we are all very cheerful and content” (L 20.11.74). They were all truly living up to their vocation.

11. SAMPIERDARENA. Hospital

The hospital was still being built and already people spoke of the FSA as the Sisters who would be called to work there; rumours reached Mother Rosa, who welcomed them, nourishing in prayer the hope that this dream of hers would come true. “Here it is a question of opening the hospital; I have had a formal promise that the Daughters of Saint Anne will be adopted”, wrote Fr Luigi Decavi from Sampierdarena on 2 June 1871. The same a week later: “Good news about the hospital”, and at the end of the year: “All well under way”. Likewise Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti, superior of the local educational and welfare Institute: “As for the hospital, the Secretary is in our favour” (L 22.5.1872). Certainty that the FSA had been chosen came with the Town Council's resolution. Proceedings began, presumably in December 1873, since on 24 January 1874 the Mother wrote to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: “I have had a letter from the Mayor of S. Pier d'Arena telling me to send him the Superior at once. So get ready and leave at once with the (Sisters) I told you” (L 183). On 2 February the Superior, already at her post, went

with Fr Antonio Accinelli to the hospital for the first contacts. Naturally, given the importance of the event, both hastened to report to her in Rome. Fr Accinelli: “...the Mayor was there, the Council, the doctor... everything was settled without the slightest opposition; there was even talk of setting up two chapels, one near the entrance, in the form of a cupboard, for Sunday Mass, and the other in a suitable place more convenient for the nuns, to reserve the Blessed Sacrament, the place not yet fixed. The stipend was set at £ 450 (each) for seven nuns, plus heating and seasoning, that is, oil... no formal contract has been made so far, but one will be before they take final possession. They have set the opening for the first of March”. The Superior repeats more or less the same things, stressing the duties to be entrusted to the Sisters. The Mother replies (L 187), suggesting the Sisters she thinks suitable for the various offices but leaving her full freedom to take from the Houses those she considers most suitable. The subject of choosing Sisters will often recur in the letters as needs arise, because Sr. A. Francesca always wants to submit her choices and opinions to the Mother's sound judgement (L 187; 190; 194; etc.).

On 26 February the President, Nicolò Montano, informed the Mother: “The Superior has already been busy for some days (and the Sisters with her) putting the hospital premises in order... the inauguration of this hospital will be celebrated on the second Sunday of March, and patients will be admitted in the following days”.

The Sisters, at first guests of the Institute at Sampierdarena, went to the hospital every day to do their work; later, though not yet provided with necessities, they settled there and worked hard to prepare what was needed for the inauguration: sewing sheets, pillowcases and gowns for the doctors, marking everything, arranging the linen room; buying what was needed for the kitchen and cleaning; sewing and hanging curtains and, to finish, an inventory of everything and a general clean. Back-breaking work. They lost two nights' sleep over it. The correspondence between the Mother and Sr. A. Francesca in February and March 1874 deals largely with organizing and starting the hospital. She entrusted this work to Sr. A. Francesca, the most experienced and one of the dearest of her collaborators. She cares greatly about its success, convinced that the Institute's good name depends on it precisely in places where God's work is opposed and malevolent voices are raised,

or at least prejudiced, because of the by now sadly notorious “Ricchini lawsuit”. On 21 February she urges Francesca: “For charity's sake, do not forget to go to the Archbishop to receive his blessing and let him know that you are the superior of the hospital; this only for the good of the poor Institute, which badly needs it” (L 198); and she advises another indispensable step: “When the inauguration ceremonies are over, see about having the Archbishop come; tell the Mayor that one is obliged to inform him whenever a chapel is opened, and so go and invite him, asking him to come and bless the hospital and the little chapel; tell Fr Accinelli to ask him too. I hope all will go well”. She returns to this point several times (L 198; 207; 227; 235; 249; etc.). To guarantee good order and success, she is peremptory and insistent on the need for a contract with the hospital (L 187; 198; 202; 207; 218; etc.).

The inauguration, on 15 March 1874, was solemn. The highest authorities of Sampierdarena and Genoa took part, with distinguished personages and “a great crowd of people”. The Sisters' work was evident and much praised. They, poor things, dead tired from working at night too, were at last left alone when the celebrations were over, longing for silence and quiet. “Today we are a little quieter and have really lived as a community, for until now it has been a time of republic” (Sr. A. Francesca to M. Rosa: 17.3.74). The Mother, sharing her Daughters' satisfaction: “Thanks be to God, author and maker of all good... All good for Him alone; we want no other. Is that not so?” (L 227).

All well, and ever better. The Sisters gain experience and self-assurance. One of them even learned to extract teeth, provided with the necessary instruments. “The Director has bought the instruments specially for Sr. A. Candida and is very pleased with the Sisters” (L 285, n. 1). “You cannot imagine – the Mother replied to Sr. A. Francesca – how advantageous this work of the Sisters will be for the Institute; word will spread and everyone will drop the bad opinion that the Daughters of Saint Anne were good for nothing” (ibid.). And she wanted other Sisters to learn; there was need in other hospitals (L 285; 288; 289; 305; 342).

People continue to speak well of the good Sisters of the hospital; the local press too praises the Institute of the FSA (L 316). At the root of her Daughters' good work Mother Rosa laid solid foundations: “Observance of the Rules is the pivot of our ac-

tions... it is the sweet bond of perfection, which helps us, one with another, to run along that dear path of peace and union”. Only in fidelity to the spirit of the Institute “do we build on solid ground and not on sand, so that our buildings may last for eternity” (L 259).

12. CORTEMAGGIORE. House of home nurses

Mother Rosa wrote to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa from Rome on 21 February 1874: “Listen, I would like you to do something for me with all ingenuity and prudence: sound out Sr. A. Teresa tactfully (she was at Genoa in the nurses' house and therefore under Fr Accinelli's jurisdiction, cf. Index III) and keep her ready for me, as I need her to put her in a house as superior. I am now writing to Insani about the contract and shall send the power of attorney to Sr. A. Tommasina (Viterbo), only to sign” (L 198).

This is the house of Maddalena Parmigiani, a lady of fifty, who had decided to give her house at Cortemaggiore, Via S. Francesco 58, to Mother Rosa so that she could place in it a community to nurse the sick at home in that town. The lady reserved for herself “the use of the property for the rest of her natural life”; she was therefore to live in the house and be cared for by the Sisters. The deed of sale was signed by Sr. A. Vincenza, with the Mother's power of attorney, on 10 March 1874. – “Today, then, you will sign the contract; God be blessed; I long for the Sisters to be there. I hope all will go well” (L 219) –. But Signora Maddalena let the Mother know through Canon Stefano Insani that she wished the Sisters' arrival to be fixed “for Easter, as she had paid her maid until then” (L Insani to M. Rosa: 17.2.74). That year Easter fell on 5 April.

The four Sisters went there on 1 April, accompanied by Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino, who reported to the Mother, writing in detail the instructions given to Signora Maddalena about her rights and duties in relation to the community (L 1.4.1874). She received full approval: “As regards Maddalena, you did well” (L 237).

The Sisters soon began their service. By 20 April they already had “three patients to nurse in their homes”, and the number soon grew: “as for patients, now that the town has begun to know us, we always have so many that we cannot even count them

all” (the superior Sr. A. Teresa to M. Rosa: 30 April '74). Two days earlier the Archpriest, Fr Domenico Costa, had written in his turn: “The Daughters of Saint Anne in the Maddalena house are doing very well. For some time now they have been called to various families to nurse their sick, so they are more cheerful and content. Tomorrow, or next Thursday at the latest, I shall go and say Mass in their house and leave the Blessed Sacrament there, which they so desire. Saint Anne blesses all these daughters of hers at Cortemaggiore. They are living up to their mission”. Providence, however, was lacking. People gave nothing because they thought the Sisters were maintained by Signora Maddalena; but once they knew the true situation they began “to bring little things; the largest gift was £ 5, but I hope that as time goes on providence will continue more” (the same to M. Rosa: 9 August '74). And so it was: “Our Lady has provided for us well; Signora Camisa (Sr. A. Francesca's mother) sent 4 bushels of wheat, another lady one bushel, and then one brought cheese, another pasta, another butter, another lard, and someone even brought bread” (the same: 16.8). This united and happy community too had its painful moment. To put an end to malicious rumours – it was said in the town that the hospital superior was improperly passing hospital goods to the superior of the Maddalena House – the Mother forbade her to go to the hospital (L 327 and 328). Later would come the cross of “Signora Maddalena”, a presence that weighed heavily on the community because of her demands. (Cf. AFSA, Lawsuits Maddalena Parmigiani).

13. INVORIO INFERIORE (AL)

Boarding school – Elementary School for boys and girls

This house had an unusual beginning. It had been opened by Fr Giovanni Boffetti, Provost of Vespolate (AL), as the seat of a women's Congregation he intended to found, taking in about ten young women of his parish, natives of Vespolate, whom he directed spiritually.

Under the guidance of the only native of Invorio, who acted as superior, they had already lived in community for a year, their activity being the education of a few boarders who also lived in the house. The good Provost realized the responsibility

this institution entailed for him and the difficulties caused by its distance from Vespolate, where he carried out his pastoral duties in his own Parish with zeal and commitment. Having heard of Mother Rosa Gattorno, he wished to entrust that work to two of her religious as “directors” and invited her to meet him there. The Mother went to Vespolate on 14 September 1874 (L 320), then went on with the Provost to Novara to confer with the Vicar General for Nuns, and finally reached Invorio; she assessed the place and the work and telegraphed Sr. A. Vincenza to send Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti and Sr. A. Gesuina Moroni as soon as possible. The next day she went to Gozzano, where the Bishop of Novara, Mgr Giacomo Gentile, was expecting her, and the same day she hastened to tell her secretary the outcome of the meeting: “So there is a house of the Daughters of Saint Anne here and the chapel must soon be set up, and you will send me the picture of Saint Anne...” (L 321); she also told her of the arrival of a postulant she had accepted. In four days of talks, agreements and negotiations she “settled everything” in accordance with what she had put to the Vicar for Nuns and the Bishop: the acceptance of the Parish Priest's six “nuns” among the Daughters of Saint Anne and the need for them to leave for the Mother House, where they would receive suitable formation. She then went to Ovada. Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti, superior of the new house, had a good deal to do in putting the premises in order and initiating the “nuns” into the customs and spirit of the Institute. All were willing, but the transition from the recent past to the new situation was not easy. To Fr Giovanni too, as to others among his friends and supporters of the local institution, the change seemed too rapid. It was therefore decided to keep the young women there for some time longer; they would receive the habit of the Daughters of Saint Anne at Invorio after suitable preparation, including the Spiritual Exercises, and would then leave. Mother Rosa agreed. “Listen, you would need to send her the form for the clothing, because the Bishop wishes to clothe those six at Invorio, where they are now; then they will send them straight to Piacenza and you will send them others. I shall let you know beforehand” (L 330). The chapel therefore had to be properly prepared: “Do send an alb; I shall send the rest from here” (ibid.). The clothing ceremony took place on 29 October 1874.

On 22 October Sr. A. Eletta Bruschi had arrived for the boarding school and the school, together with another Sister. After the new novices had left, the premises had to be prepared for the works: the boarding school

and the school with two sections, boys and girls. Documents had to be prepared and submitted for government authorization of both activities, and a flat refusal for the school was rightly feared, since not only equipment but also premises were lacking.

“It is true – Superior Bucciotti wrote to the Mother – that the house has wonderful air and a beautiful position, but that is not enough to be in order; it means that God will provide” (29.10.74). Government approval came, since at first there was only one mixed-age class of 10 pupils. It was held on the ground floor, in the room that served “as refectory and workroom for the Sisters”. But a way was soon found of making two rooms for the school. To these “ordinary” activities at home the Sisters added the teaching of catechism in the Parish.

It was certainly a great consolation to the Mother, at the end of 1874, to hear the testimony of the Parish Priest, who declared himself “edified by the harmony of the Sisters”, a testimony that had become general in Invorio; and the fruits of that holy and praised harmony were seen at the end of the school year. At the examinations and display, boarders and pupils showed what they had learned in the various subjects of the syllabus and their artistic abilities in singing and reciting poetry. Praise for teachers and pupils, prizes for the most deserving, joyful surprise for all: “Who would ever have thought to see such things in Invorio!”.

AFSA. F 30; F 35; FcIS. Invorio Inferiore.

14. TERRICCIOLA (PI). Boarding school – School

At Terricciola, as in so many other farming centres, there was no well-organized and well-run school able to guarantee children a sound Christian basic education, so the Archpriest, Fr Secondo Griselli, and with him many fathers and mothers, wished to found an Elementary school run by Religious. The plan had already been made known and had gained concrete support. The Institute to approach was suggested by Fr Alessandro Mancini SJ. He had come to know the Foundress and her daughters while preaching the Spiritual Exercises in the Mother House (L 232) and had directed several young women wishing to embrace religious life there (L 315). The Archpriest therefore wrote to Mother Rosa on 10 June 1874, describing the situation of the place, asking for

her collaboration and setting out the terms and treatment to be given to the Sisters for their service. The Mother replied in the affirmative on the 14th (the date is deduced from the addressee's letter; this and her other letters to Griselli are missing). Taking note of her acceptance, the Archpriest later told her the date of the Sisters' arrival, 15 November at the latest, since lengthy works to make the premises sound were in progress.

Mother Rosa mentions this place on 25 September, writing from Genoa to Sr. A. Vincenza: “You must go to Terricciola and S. Martinello” (L 329); then to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: “Sr. A. Vincenza leaves tomorrow” (4 November '74) (L 349); and finally to Fr Agostino Donadio: “Sr. A. Vincenza has left for Terricciola, and I have already had news that she was received with singing and enthusiasm” (L 351). On the day of arrival and the days following, she and the four Sisters were guests of the Archpriest, Fr Secondo Griselli, because the house intended for their dwelling and the school was not finished; windows, sanitation and other finishings were missing; but Sr. A. Vincenza insisted that at least one room be finished as soon as possible so that they could withdraw: “What a penance in someone else's house – she confided to the Mother – but we are surrounded with kindness”. Among so much good news she writes enthusiastically: “Today, Sunday, the Archpriest, explaining the Gospel, presented us to the people; the name of the Daughters of Saint Anne rang through the church; he said we had left all our dearest ones to save their children... he told them: I leave them under your protection; let them lack nothing”. On 10 November she and the superior, Sr. A. Beatrice Merici, were taken to the Bishop, Mgr Ferdinando Capponi, at Volterra. The account of this visit too is fine and full of news; but the letter also has its sad note: “The work is making no progress; imagine, there is only one man working, with two women carrying stones and making lime... there is more than a month's work... let us hope that next Saturday (14 November) we can move into some room”. The Mother answers her promptly (L 352; 357; 359).

Meanwhile the Archpriest goes on furnishing the house. The Sisters for their part prepare to organize their work well. There is already the first boarder, a capable and good girl; many future pupils are impatiently awaiting the opening of the school, which the Archpriest wants to be grand, with a fine dinner for the pupils. On 19 November Sr. A. Vincenza leaves, because, as

the Mother had told her (L 359), she must meet that same day at Florence station the Sisters she is to accompany to S. Martinello. She leaves the Sisters sorry and a little anxious, but she is at peace: they are in good hands. On 26 November the excellent Archpriest reassures her about the Sisters' present and future: “On Saturday (21 Nov.) your good Sisters took up residence in their house, which, thanks to the efforts of the lawyer Lami, has become most respectable and provided with every comfort”.

The Superior writes to the Mother: “We have started the girls' school; there is a good number, more than 80, and besides there are young women of 25-30... almost all are Children of Mary, all devoted; they receive communion every day. Next Thursday the boys' school will open too, so we shall have three schools (classes)”. This morning our (community) timetable also began. The Archpriest echoes her: “Thanks be to the Lord, the schools are well started, and the charitable services of the Daughters of Saint Anne are constant and have won them the goodwill and approval of all the people. For the present they are not as well provided for as one would wish, but Providence is helping us, and I hope we shall be able to do much better as time goes on” (L 20.1.1875).

15. S. MARTINELLO-PERUGIA. Elementary School

The Marchioness Edvige Spinola, who intended to open a school for the education of children of the poor class, had been advised by her friend the Marchioness Agnese di Sora Piombino to turn to Mother Rosa Gattorno, whom she knew well, since she had opened a school at Foligno. And it was during one of her visits to Foligno, in May 1874, that the Mother had gone to S. Martinello (S. Martino ai Colli) to see the place, meet the Marchioness, learn her plans and wishes for the school and agree on the time of opening (L 262). She later told Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino that she would have to go there after opening the Terricciola house (L 321; 329). And finally, having told her the date of departure, 19 November 1874 (L 359), she gave her precise instructions about the new foundation: “The Marchioness (Edvige Spinola) has written to me saying that as soon as you arrive she will give you fr. 50 for the month of November, although it is already

begun and well advanced, and you will find everything else, so she tells me. Tell her that if she is not satisfied with any of the religious she should write to me and we will make an exchange, and likewise if anything is not to her liking she should tell me frankly, for I will try to satisfy her in everything” (L 361). Sr. A. Vincenza, having got the superior Eufemia Camporesi and the three Sisters started and advised them, left for Foligno as the Mother had told her. The report she surely made, with her usual precision and care, has not been preserved. There is a letter from the Superior, brief but effective in its brevity, on the situation in the first days: “I have no words to describe how happy I am at S. Martinello and what courtesy and attentions the Marchioness shows us. She is always thinking of us and is very fond of us, being so pleased with the schools, both for the number of pupils – we already have more than two hundred – and for what they are taught, and she is especially mad about the singing; and the Marquis goes everywhere singing their praises. Dear Mother, pray the Lord that I may go on satisfying them” (2.12.1874).

Later, however, there was no lack of privation and poverty, since the Marchioness's subsidy was not enough and the Mother had to support the Sisters, who not only did not lose heart but found ways of extending, as far as possible, the reach of their charity, visiting and nursing the sick of the surrounding area.

16. LUGO (RA). Elementary School

The request for the Daughters of Saint Anne for this school was sent to Mother Rosa by the “Opera Pia Emaldi” on 5 November 1874, signed by Count Tommaso Emaldi. She was asked to “accept the direction and running of the Elementary School, providing three teachers, two of them certified”, as soon as possible, since 120 pupils, “the autumn holidays” being over, were waiting for the school to reopen. Negotiations concluded (L 346; 368), the Mother announced the date of the Sisters' departure and the names of the two certified teachers (L 382). Accompanied by Sr. A. Vincenza, the two Sisters left, as agreed, on 28 December 1874. The next day Sr. A. Vincenza wrote the Mother an enthusiastic letter. The welcome from the Counts – Raffaele, his sister, his mother (Countess Maria) – was most festive. “The house is enormous”, four

fine bedrooms with a curtained bed each, a parlour, refectory, laundry, cellar, a small kitchen garden, a large chapel with two altars and the confessional, four large classrooms “which they told us will be full of girls, so, Mother, you must send two nuns as soon as possible”. This house was not born in straitened circumstances like the others; not only is it well set up and ready, it also has an educational tradition: that of the “Filippine Mothers”, who had run the school and were obliged to leave for reasons of their own. The “gentlemen of the Congregation” with whom she conferred told her clearly that they want “their method” to be followed. And Sr. A. Vincenza thought it wise to agree “for the moment”, she explains to the Mother, “then little by little we shall see about doing things our way”. It is decided that the schools will open on Monday of the following week: 5 January 1875. The Mother approves but reminds her that she must hurry, for there are other houses to open: “the people of Mercatello have written and are begging us to go there...; so I have fixed the 10th of January” (L 395). Thus the last letter of 1874 closes an intense year and opens onto the new one with dynamic impetus towards the future.
