PRESENTATION

At the dawn of this century Mother Rosa Gattorno returned to the Father's house; but she left behind her great family — the Daughters of Saint Anne — made up of about 4,000 sisters present in 368 houses in Italy and in many foreign countries.

The second millennium is fast drawing to its close, and we can see ever more clearly that the seed Mother Rosa planted in the heart of the Church has continued to bear fruit, multiplying the signs of a vigorous and powerful vitality.

Consecrated Life, indeed, precisely in the Church, with the Church and for the Church, shows itself to be an authentic and generous gift of the Spirit who works wonders.

And it is also through commitment in daily life, admirably expressed in this simple correspondence, that we are most often able to grasp its «edifying» presence.

That is why the fourth volume — from 1875 to 1877 — of the Letters of Mother Rosa Gattorno now sees the light. Others will follow, setting the rhythm of the silent path to holiness of a great woman of faith.

Reading these letters immerses us, indeed, in the secret of feelings that could not otherwise be perceived.

Mother Rosa would never have imagined or suspected that anyone could reveal the richness of her humanity, expressed wholly and without pause in the everyday ordinariness of her life.

The collection of Letters that make up this fourth volume brings out, in my view, one of the fundamental elements that permeate the whole spirituality of Rosa Gattorno: her being, and always wanting to be, a MOTHER.

And it is an authentic motherhood, full, attentive, difficult, paid for and suffered in silence.

In the Letters Rosa reveals herself fully for what she is, a mother twice over: of her Institute and of her children Alessandro and Carlotta.

For her sisters, in fact, she feels herself a true mother; she follows their lives and their personal circumstances, and mourns their deaths. She is attentive to the needs of the various communities. With tenderness and wonder she records the growth of her Institute, «which was born so recently».

Her language, always restrained and spare, manages to show the heart of a woman who is the first to live the Gospel.

Many times we can read between the lines her readiness to offer her life for her daughters, such that it allows her to express in the first

person, always with clear points of reference, certain characteristics of Consecrated Life that must always be evident in every Daughter of Saint Anne: inner and outer humility, unceasing prayer, charity without bounds.

Her exhortations to her daughters are not limited to sayings such as «be cheerful and you will live» or «Jesus is calling you and you must answer at once»; at times they are laden with sadness and serene truth, as when she writes «You have been the cause of extreme sorrow to me».

But Rosa Gattorno's tenderness rises highest when she writes to her son, or about her son Alessandro and her daughter Carlotta.

Rosa never forgot the children of her flesh, never shut them out of her immense affection.

To Alessandro she expresses the worries of every mother.

Only by reading her writings can one realise that Gattorno's inner stature is the simple, homely stature of every mother on earth.

She is worried about the bad company her son may keep.

She is anguished because she cannot find work for Alessandro, who is now twenty years old.

She longs for him to join some Catholic Association, to give points of reference to his journey of faith and so that he may be committed to a clear Christian witness.

In Rosa Gattorno's soul there throbs the same anxiety as in every Christian mother who watches, fearful and proud, her child grow up.

Her love is not part of a chapter of her life now closed, as though the call to Consecrated Life had erased the features of her human motherhood; it is happily and indissolubly joined to her responsibility as Foundress of a great religious family. To Sister Anna Francesca, whom she had entrusted with looking after Alessandro, she writes stressing the delicacy of the task: «Don't let it be noticed».

And again, drawing the sisters into her motherly anxiety, in May 1876 she writes: «We are all thinking of you, Alessandro... How many prayers your poor Mother!... My dear son... One day you will see whether I have thought of you».

And in a letter to a sister whom she had not allowed to be present at her brother's death, causing her enormous suffering, she will voice, offering herself as an example, all her anguish as a mother over the illness of her distant son: «He is my son. I am a mother».

And so to her daughter Carlotta, whom she almost always calls tenderly Carlottina, she will give all the time needed for her difficult growing up, and with a joy she never hid she will personally see to her marriage.

But Rosa Gattorno never ceases to astonish those who have the adventure, or rather the grace, of meeting her.

Ninety-four years after her death she continues to be a generous mother, and will surely be so more and more.

While the Bishops of the Church gather in Synod next November to reflect more deeply on the gift of Consecrated Life, I am glad to think of the youngest of the offspring born of the charism and heart of Mother Rosa Gattorno, the Sons of Saint Anne, whom I myself have had the privilege of accompanying in their growth since their birth.

These Letters of the Mother have unforgettable accents for everyone, but I hope that they may be an expression of motherly tenderness directed especially to the very dear Sons of Saint Anne.

Mgr. Natalino Zagotto

INTRODUCTION

In continuity with the earlier volumes, the present one offers a further block of the letters of Mother Rosa Gattorno for the three years 1875-1877, made up of 429 letters registered in the Archive of the Daughters of Saint Anne, Generalate, Rome. Many others from this period are mentioned in the correspondence of the time, but unfortunately they have not been preserved. In our opinion, however, they would have added nothing new or substantially different to those in our possession, which form a valuable historical record opening onto a range of very important facts, situations and events of those three years, and at the same time give us an autobiographical outline of the Mother scattered with points of light: fleeting revelations of states of mind, feelings, the deep motives of her action, raisings of the heart to God, the one good and the one reason for her being and her working. It is these points of light that give value to the brevity of three years, undoubtedly too few in relation to the whole historical development of the Institute. But set as they are in the period «of grace» of the beginnings, they concentrate the bursting, dynamic force of the charism. The Foundress, wholly taken up with the awareness of her own vocation-mission, gives herself entirely to the Work of God. Her universal vision of «urgent charity» finds new paths and opens onto ever new horizons in «new fields» to be cultivated. And ever new and more numerous «labourers» knock at the door of Saint Anne.

From 1866 to 1874, 24 houses had been opened. From '75 to '77 no fewer than 27 were opened, not counting the many others requested from various places and by various bodies that were left unanswered for various reasons. The Daughters of Saint Anne, inspired by her, press on swiftly and courageously from northern and central Italy to the «far south». In 1876 they are at Agrigento, the first seed of an unimaginable, prodigious flowering on Sicilian soil, and then at other key points of an equally surprising spread in other regions: Maratea (Potenza), Naples, Bovino (Foggia). Mother Rosa feels the weight of so much activity: «A sea of business and worries» (L 392) and «She does not know which to deal with first» (L 144). «I would need a hundred arms to do everything that is needed» (L 94). In 1875 (3 April) she lost the precious help of her beloved, faithful and diligent secretary Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino. And five months later she also lost another beloved and faithful daughter of the first hour: Sr. A. Francesca Camisa. Meanwhile Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega was being trained to replace Sr. A. Vincenza. To her she confides: «So much work!» (L 367); and to Sr. A. Santina Solenghi, one of the new collaborators: «The many tasks

leave me not a minute's freedom» (L 368). The secret of so much work, heavy for her precarious health but very fruitful in good results, is expressed in passing, with a kindly reproach, to Sr. A. Benedetta, who, having something urgent to tell her, went into her room one evening and dared to rouse her from her absorption in God: «I have only the night; by day I am always in the midst of business!» (L 408).

In the night, wholly and only for God, she offers herself in adoration, pleads, and obtains everything from the Father for the Work of Saint Anne. «I have no other treasure than prayer, and with it I obtain all my courage; one day we shall find our labours at the throne of God the judge» (L 10).

The Work is His: the Father's; He takes care of it and provides. In 1876, Cardinal Protector Luigi Vannicelli having died, Cardinal Giuseppe Berardi was appointed. To him she presents once more the long-standing problems: the approval of the Rules and the related recognition of the Institute; the readmission of Father Tornatore (L 183). And from the new «Cardinal Protector» comes a most consoling reply. He tells her on 30 April 1876: «Yesterday the S. Congregation of Bishops and Regulars sent the Bishop of Piacenza the decree of praise together with the observations on the Rules». As for Fr Tornatore, she will be able to avail herself of his enlightened teaching, his counsel and his ever precious help in forming the Daughters of the Holy Mother and in guiding the Institute. The New Year circular letters to the whole Family (L 224 and 227) are signed by both, Foundress and Co-founder, and in the correspondence too the Father is referred to as one «of the family» (cf. Indice 111,2).

In that same April, on the 26th, Carlotta married Count Gaspare Barbiellini Amidei (L 183,8). Having «settled her honourably in society» is a satisfaction for her mother and for all the relatives. She shares the news with Alessandro, in Argentina, still struggling with a hard reality impervious to his hopes (L 197). He will soon return to Italy, disillusioned and in debt. And his mother will go on suffering with her Alessandro the pain of his unemployment (L 267, n. 1; 411,3). It is a sorrow that opens space for her self-giving in the Work of God.

Now that the Institute has its full place in the Church, she continues on her way, living what she teaches her Daughters: «Courage, my daughter, for it is time to work and carry out great missions, to win souls for God!... Courage, blood for blood; Jesus on the cross is all torn, and so are we, aren't we?» (L 274).

She had received the invitation to send her daughters to the distant Americas; and she was already preparing them for the great missions, overseas.

Sister Anna Catterina.2 You are asked to remind the sisters to offer suffrages as the Rule requires in Chap. 5, Article 6, that is, to apply for each of them three Communions and three recitations of the Rosary said in common, and to hear Holy Mass three times.

  1. We hope that the prayers of the rather large number of sisters who make up the Family of our glorious holy Mother Saint Anne, Mother of Mary Immaculate, will soon bring our Departed into Paradise.

  2. At present the Institute numbers twenty-three houses and three hundred sisters; in the year just ended, 1874, six houses were founded,3 and in 1875, barely begun, there are already requests. To whom, sisters, do we owe so rapid a spread of the Institute in the few years since its birth? Surely to the mercy of the Heavenly Father, who has been pleased to bless it.

  3. In general the sisters are animated by the spirit of their vocation; they keep continually before their eyes the end for which the Lord has raised them to the great nobility of being Daughters

of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate; and that end is to consecrate their whole life to blessing Him, thanking Him and praising Him for all the wonders worked in their Holy Mother, and for the greatest of them all, that of having made her Mother of the Immaculate, His Mother Mary Most Holy, and to imitate her in all her virtues, which are taught us by our holy Rules.

  1. Above all, three points serve to attain this end: first, punctuality in rising, so that as soon as they hear the five o'clock bell they get up at once, without letting even a moment pass. Second, that at half past five they are all already in the chapel to begin meditation;4 and third, never to speak alone with persons of the other sex, and not to fail in that point of the Rule on modesty which forbids touching one another even in play.5

  2. If in the few years since its birth the Institute has had to mourn the loss of some Sister,6 it has been observed that this was precisely because they trampled on the three points of the Rule mentioned above.

  3. The Superiors are therefore urged to watch that the sisters are faithful in observing all the Rules, especially the three points named. Then the Heavenly Father will take His delight in our Institute and spread it everywhere.

Sr. Anna Rosa Gattorno

P.S. You are asked to read it to the Sisters.

1 The date is missing. From the practice followed in later years too for the annual «Circulars», it can be inferred that it was written in the first days of January.

2 Sr. A. Pierina Tea, Sr. A. Emilia Dedamo, Sr. A. Michelina Morelli, Sr. A. Elena Bianchi, Sr. A. Caterina Palladini.

3 Houses opened in 1874: Sampierdarena, hospital; Cortemaggiore, home nursing of the sick; Invorio Inferiore, boarding school and school; Terricciola, boarding school and school; S. Martinello, school. Cf. Lettere 3, pp. 764-774.

4 The daily timetable laid down: rising at 5; at 5.30 in chapel for meditation lasting three quarters of an hour; at 6.15 Holy Mass followed by half an hour of thanksgiving (AFSA, 61 IcO. 4).

5 The 1869 Rule sets out the prescriptions on the relations mentioned here in Chapter 4, on chastity, and Chapter 5, on the virtue of modesty.

6 Several Sisters had not persevered in their vocation: either they had gone back to their families of their own accord, or they had been sent away.

She suggests that prayers be offered that she may be freed from giving evidence under oath in the lawsuit with Ricchino. She urges the departure of some Sisters, who will soon be replaced.

A.M.F.

My Francesca,

  1. Today I received your letter in which you told me so many lovely things, and in particular it was very dear to me to hear that the Rosary is said in the hospital.2 My God! What consolation I felt, you certainly cannot imagine it.

  2. Listen: for a month have it said for the oaths I have to take, that God may free me from them by letting me win the lawsuit, which agitates me not a little when I think of it.3 What torment it is! I hear from the lawyer Boccardo that it will soon be heard. Alas! May God touch the hearts of those judges so that they annul the oaths; everything is obtained through prayer.4

  3. Send me quickly the sisters I asked you for in my letter, because I need them so much.5 Sr. A. Vincenza has been expecting them since Monday; for charity's sake, because, as I told you, by the 9th of this month you must send me Sr. A. Battistina, and she can come alone, but these two quickly. I have already written to Fr Accinelli, who I hope will not pull any faces, because on Thursday I shall send him three or four good ones,6 so if you want some too I shall send them to you. Meanwhile you can send him that fussy one you mention.7

  4. Listen, I want you to find out for me in which Church the Dominican Father was when he said those things; tell mamma a little about what he said, she will know well what he said; otherwise I shall have a way of finding out. If you can go to Genoa for a little, I should like it, because I should

like to know whether he is from Rome or one of those from Castello or Bologna.8

  1. You will tell me it is curiosity, but it may be useful to me for certain plans of mine concerning the Institute at this time. Oh! how many tribulations! It seems that these days they are being emptied out by the sackful.

  2. I hear you are unwell again. What pain you give me, dear daughter; take care of yourself. Make a quick trip here and you will get better; for pity's sake, it is too cold now, so much snow, so much ice.

Goodbye, your Affect. M. I am in a hurry.

7. Listen a moment: have the Superior of the House send me the dispatch note for the candles.9 What a pity, I fear they have been lost. They tell me they have the note. Thank you for the basket, but I don't want it so often. Do you understand?

1 The date in the original letter has been corrected, the month written as no. 1 being struck out and replaced by no. 2. The letter, however, is clearly from January, given the context.

2 On 31 December the Superior had written to her: «In this novena of the Child Jesus we have begun to say the Rosary, and every evening each Sister (in each of the wards) leads the Rosary and all the patients answer her... you can see that they do it gladly.»

3 Cf. L 24, n. 6.

4 The lawyer Domenico Boccardo, counsel in the case, was the uncle of Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino.

5 On 30 December 1874 she had asked her to send off Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi, Sr. A. Stanislaa Vignoli and two other Sisters. Cf. Lettere 3, L 394,3. Sr. A. Vincenza was to take them to Mercatello, the new house. Cf. L 4,5.

6 Fr Accinelli did not hesitate to voice his displeasure when Sisters were transferred from the Genoa House, because it seemed to him that the home nursing of the sick would suffer, since the new Sisters were generally less experienced than the others.

7 A Sister who was not behaving well.

8 Listen, I want... Bologna. Sr. A. Francesca had written to her that a Dominican friar in a church in Genoa, during his Advent preaching, had praised the Daughters of Saint Anne for their work. The Mother wants to know who he is for particular reasons concerning the Institute.

9 The Superior of the «House», as the Institute in Sampierdarena was usually called, had told her that candles were being sent for the chapel of the Mother House. Cf. L 3. But Sr. A. Francesca had not thought it wise to send them, because of the excessive cost; she wrote to tell her so on 5 January.

She regrets that the parcel of candles has not arrived and wants the dispatch note so that she can have it traced. She encourages her and urges her to pray for providence.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. How sorry I am not to have received the candles yet, which were so dear to me because I needed them! The sacristan talks about them all the time; I have had them searched for everywhere, and they tell me to try to get the dispatch note and they will see about making a claim; so send it to me at once, and if you have torn it up,1 go to the railway and have it renewed, and send it to me at once.

  2. Listen, see about sending me the year's accounts; get Sr. A. Francesca to help you and send them to me.2

  3. On Wednesdays (they are all and) meat is eaten all year round, except the Wednesdays of St Joseph and those of St Anne, as our holy Rules say.3 Courage, and hope in the Lord; commend yourself to my Rosa Parodi,4 say an Our Father, Hail Mary and Glory Be to her every day, that she may send you Providence, and you will see that it will come. You cannot believe how much I suffer over it, for if I could I would certainly send you the money.5

Goodbye, my daughter, and pray, and have prayers said for the lawsuit you know of.

Your affect. M.

1 If you have torn up the dispatch note for the candles, have a duplicate made at the railway dispatch office.

2 // rendimento dell'anno = the annual balance sheet of the house.

3 On Wednesdays: the Superior had asked her whether abstinence from meat was obligatory every Wednesday.

4 Rosa Parodi, a dear friend of hers who died in the odour of sanctity, to whom she commended herself to obtain graces. Cf. Lettere 1, p.524.

5 She suffers on hearing of her Daughters' privations, and still more at not being able to help them by sending at least a little money.

She fears that the Superior of the Lugo community is not applying herself diligently to running the work, and asks her to give her suitable advice. She tells her of the arrival of two Sisters for Lugo and of others whom she will take to Mercatello.

A.M.F.

My dearest daughter,

  1. I received your long letter yesterday, in which you gave me the finest news.1 Blessed be God! I enclose one from your Mother; I cannot understand why this year they say nothing to you about what they usually send you every year. What can it be?2

  2. Listen, say something to Edvige: I have found that at Poss's she let everything in the factory go anyhow. She no longer even bothered to see whether the girls were being entered, no longer keeping a check on the register. In short, it is clear, as everyone says, that she no longer went to the factory; it was a real bazaar.3 My dear, you will hear the rest by word of mouth.

  3. I would not want her to do the same in that house; it worries me a great deal, because I fear she may hatch schemes with this white one who you tell me has been assigned as Confessor;4 so put Sr. A. Enrichetta in as overseer and tell her to write to me often; leave her a little paper too, and as many stamps as you like.5

  4. Tell her not to trust herself, and to note that all those who have indulged in certain whims have repented and are now asking forgiveness; so, for charity's sake, mind you keep a close watch. My dear, what you tell me about Sr. A. Adelaide is perfectly true: it is true, they think of themselves and let others think of the rest.6 Fi-

nally, tell her she must keep the accounts properly, both income and expenditure, and send them to me every six months; I insist on it.

  1. Listen, the two Sisters for there will be with you on the 7th of this month, I cannot manage earlier; the others will be at Castel Bolognese on the 11th of this month, on the same train you arrived by.7 Do me the kindness of writing how much you spent and what seats you took, so that I know what to do in sending these two to Lugo; it will also be useful to me for Pesaro.

  2. In this way you will meet at the station. You will be alone, but only for a few hours; I think I have explained myself, if there is time. Write to me and I shall try to explain better.

  3. It is bitterly cold here; I am well and have had no further sign of fainting, but I do not stir from my little study because my head is something else: this year it freezes easily and immediately starts to ache.8

Goodbye, yours for all ages,

affect. and close M. R.

1 Sr. A. Vincenza, who had gone to Lugo with two Sisters to start the new work, had written to her on 1 January with news: the kindly welcome of the Bishop, Mgr. Luigi Tesorieri, at Imola, where Count Raffaele Emaldi had accompanied them; the order of the house; the community timetable.

2 A letter from Sr. A. Vincenza's mother had arrived in Piacenza. In giving her this news M. Rosa asks her why her parents have not yet sent her the usual gift of money as in other years.

3 In the letter mentioned above Sr. A. Vincenza had expressed her doubts about Sr. A. Edvige Moroncini's suitability for the office of Superior. The Mother tells her to advise and admonish her, pointing out that in Piacenza, as directress of the girl workers at the Poss factory, she had been negligent, failing to enter the girls in the registers and neglecting supervision. Real disorder had resulted.

4 Her fears about the Superior are heightened by the doubts Sr. A. Vincenza expressed about the confessor assigned by the Bishop, a Dominican father: «I learned that there are Priests here who try to take nuns away and send them to other Institutes». The Mother fears the Superior may let herself be led astray by the Dominican (the white one).

5 Put Sr. A. Enrichetta Salvatela in as overseer. The overseer or councillor corresponds to the present office of assistant to the Superior. Cf. Appi.Reg. Del. Chap. 6, 2, 2.

6 What you tell me is perfectly true: «This Superior — Sr. A. Vincenza wrote — has all the ways of Sister Adelaide: she is very exact about herself, but not about the house».

7 The Sisters who were to go with her to Mercatello (Pesaro) would leave on the 11th; she would join them on the train at Castel Bolognese and go on with them to Pesaro.

8 non mi muovo d'incamerino, I do not leave my little study, where there was a wood-burning stove. ...mi viene a far male: the cold gave her headaches.

She tells her to send off a Sister and asks her to send 100 francs to cover the expenses of journeys and clothings. She has no one else to turn to.

A.M.F.

My Francesca, dearer than all

  1. Listen, you will have received the telegram not to send the religious from Genoa any more, but by the 9th of this month you will send me Sr. A. Battistina alone;1 and then I should like to ask you, if you can, to send me F. 100 by the 6th, because with these blessed dispatches and clothings I cannot tell you what it takes,2 you know already, and I fear I shall not have enough, and so I would not like to turn to anyone. You know I have no one, especially here in this ugly city.

  2. I should also like (if I am not too indiscreet) you to send me two tins of paraffin;3 I hear it costs much less than here; it is really dear now.

  3. Dear daughter, what pain it is to see so many people to be kept, and it has to be done; I have no other resource than to go to church to my Eternal Father, that He may provide for me; but what can you do, I see that this good God also wants me to bestir myself wherever I best can and know how, to find the means.4 I hope you will be able to send me everything.

  4. Listen, I shall say no more for now; I am so weighed down with work that that is all; tell the House to send me the year's accounts too. The same to the one at Sestri.5

Goodbye

your affect. M. for all ages. Amen

1 Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi, a good nurse. The Mother intended to entrust her with the office of Superior at Mercatello. Cf. L 13,2.

2 Dispatches: the journeys of Sisters going to the various existing or new communities; clothings: on 28 December nine Postulants had received the FSA habit, and she had had to provide the cloth needed for the habits and meet the related expenses.

3 The paraffin was used for lighting the house.

4 The Eternal Father is her treasurer; she is convinced of it and turns to Him. But Providence has its ways and does not dispense her from seeking them with trust and diligence.

5 Tell the House: this was what they called the Institute at Sampierdarena. The one at Sestri: the Superior, Sr. A. Giacomina Schenardi.
